papers.title_in_file: Better than classical? The subtle art of benchmarking quantum machine learning models
papers.version_note: arXiv:2403.07059v2 [quant-ph], 14 Mar 2024 (dated March 15, 2024). The text layer holds the paper once.
papers.what_it_is: A large-scale benchmark study from Xanadu that tests 12 prototypical quantum machine learning models against classical baselines on 160 mostly synthetic binary classification datasets, with ablations that remove entanglement and a discussion of benchmarking pitfalls.

existing.note: The paper limits the result: not all models were tested on all datasets and benchmarks (runtime limits), and the finding holds for the small-scale datasets chosen. The abstract's wording 6 binary classification tasks creating 160 datasets is the paper's own; Section III calls the 6 items data generation procedures grouped into 10 benchmarks.
existing.value: The authors report that in a benchmark of 12 quantum machine learning models on 6 binary classification tasks creating 160 datasets, out-of-the-box classical machine learning models outperform the quantum classifiers overall; they note that not all models are tested on all datasets and benchmarks.
existing.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Section V.A, p.14; Introduction, p.2
quotes: We find that overall, out-of-the-box classical machine learning models outperform the quantum classifiers.
systematically tests 12 popular quantum machine learning models on 6 binary classification tasks used to create 160 individual datasets
Note that not all models are tested on all datasets and benchmarks
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

existing.value: The authors state that they predominantly use artificially generated data, which may limit conclusions with respect to real-world data, and that the largest circuit simulated has 18 qubits.
quotes: we predominantly use artificially generated data which allows us to understand and vary the properties and size of the datasets. This may limit conclusions with respect to “real-world” data
The largest size of a circuit simulated in the study has 18 qubits
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states its own data scope in Section III and the qubit limit in footnote 3.
existing.reader_inference: MNIST (a real dataset, downscaled) is one of the six data generation procedures, so predominantly is the paper's word, not entirely.

existing.note: The result is model dependent. Removing entanglement did not reduce accuracy of DressedQuantumCircuitClassifier, but did reduce it for QuantumBoltzmannMachine and DataReuploadingClassifier. The test was run on mnist pca up to 9 dimensions for the three QNN models that beat the separable model.
existing.value: The authors report that removing entanglement from a quantum model often results in as good or better performance, but that removing entanglement does decrease the test accuracy of QuantumBoltzmannMachine and DataReuploadingClassifier.
existing.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Section V.C, pp.15-17; Fig. 13, p.17
quotes: removing entanglement from a quantum model often results in as good or better performance
However, removing entanglement does decrease the test accuracy of QuantumBoltzmannMachine and DataReuploadingClassifier.
The DressedQuantumCircuitClassifier shows no drop in performance, while DataReuploadingClassifier, and to some extent QuantumBoltzmannMachine, do worse without entanglement.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

existing.note: Section V.B adds that on two curves diff the quantum models perform worse than the classical method as difficulty is increased, and that the claim rests on the difficulty-controlled benchmarks hyperplanes diff, hidden manifold diff and two curves diff.
existing.value: The authors report that they do not observe any improvement in performance of the quantum models relative to the classical baselines for increasing problem difficulties; on two curves diff the quantum models perform worse than the corresponding classical method as the difficulty is increased.
quotes: Secondly, we do not observe any improvement in performance of the quantum models relative to the classical baselines for increasing problem difficulties.
For the difficulty-controlled benchmark two curves diff (Appendix F), the quantum models perform worse than the corresponding classical method as the difficulty is increased.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that of 55 arXiv papers containing the terms quantum machine learning and outperform in title or abstract, about 40% claim that a quantum model outperforms a classical model, about 50% claim that an improvement to a quantum machine learning method outperforms the original one, and only 3 papers or 4% find that a quantum model does not outperform a classical one.
quotes: Out of 55 relevant papers published on the preprint server arXiv 1 until December 2023 that contain the terms “quantum machine learning” and “outperform” in title or abstract
one finds that about 40% claim that a quantum model outperforms a classical model, while about 50% claim that some improvement to a quantum machine learning method outperforms the original one
Only 3 papers or 4% find that a quantum model does not outperform
assertions.certainty_reason: A literature count by one study; the sample is keyword-selected.
assertions.reader_inference: The count is a snapshot taken until December 2023 and depends on the keyword choice.

assertions.value: The authors state that the 55 papers are a subset of 73 papers returned by the keyword search, selected by manually reading abstracts and discarding papers on quantum-inspired methods, other fields, or without an explicit method-outperforms-method statement; other search terms showed similar patterns.
quotes: The 55 papers are a subset of 73 papers returned by the keyword search, and were selected by manually reading the abstracts
Other search terms than “outperform*”, such as “better than” or “benchmark*”, were tried to detect a possible selection bias caused by the keyword search, but showed similar patterns.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own selection procedure in footnotes 1 and 2.

assertions.value: The authors report a simulated thought experiment in which 100 researchers each investigate 20 quantum models and publish only the best against a classical model; with assumed true performance of mean 0.65 (standard deviation 0.07) for classical and mean 0.55 (standard deviation 0.1) for quantum models, the published mean performance of the quantum models is 0.74 versus 0.65 for classical ones.
quotes: Consider 100 researchers, each investigating 20 different types of quantum models before settling on a promising design and publishing benchmarks of the best one against a classical model of their choice.
(say, with a mean of 0.65 and standard deviation of 0.07) than quantum ones (mean 0.55, standard deviation 0.1)
the published mean performance of the quantum models is 0.74 vs. 0.65 of classical ones
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulation under assumed normal distributions chosen by the authors; an illustration, not a measurement of the field.
assertions.reader_inference: The distribution parameters are assumptions of the authors, so the 0.74 figure illustrates the mechanism and is not an estimate of real published results.

assertions.value: The authors state that a positivity bias of this nature is not a question of ethical misconduct but is built into the research methodology of leaderboard-driven research, and that performance of a model cannot be viewed as a property that can be demonstrated by an empirical study.
quotes: a positivity bias of this nature is not a question of ethical misconduct, but built into the research methodology.
cannot be viewed as a property that can be “demonstrated” by an empirical study
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument by the authors without a measurement beyond the illustration.

assertions.value: The authors report an illustrative example in which a minor rearrangement of the data in a classification task causes an adversarially hand-crafted quantum model to switch from being nearly unable to learn to gaining perfect accuracy.
quotes: a minor rearrangement of the data in a classification task causes an – admittedly adversarially hand-crafted – quantum model to switch from being nearly unable to learn, to gaining perfect accuracy
assertions.certainty_reason: A single hand-crafted example, labeled by the authors as highly simplified.

assertions.value: The paper cites studies reporting that leaderboard rankings change when a few datasets are excluded or scores are aggregated differently (Dehghani et al.), that correcting labeling errors in the ImageNet validation set changes the ranking of models (Northcutt et al.), and that a different test-train split decreases accuracies by as much as 14% (Recht et al.), with the ranking between models largely unaffected by the split.
quotes: significantly different leaderboard rankings are obtained when excluding a few datasets from benchmarking suites or making changes to the way that scores are aggregated
find that correcting labeling errors in the ubiquitous ImageNet validation set likewise changes the ranking of models
decreases the accuracies of models by as much as 14%
Although, reassuringly, the ranking between models is largely unaffected by this intervention.
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The paper cites studies suggesting that small adjustments to transformer architectures have no measurable effect on performance, that standard convolutional neural networks still beat transformers when trained on a comparable amount of data, and that extensive hyperparameter optimisation can give baseline models of generative adversarial networks, deep reinforcement learning and Bayesian deep neural nets the performance of more advanced proposals.
quotes: small adjustments to transformer architectures advertised in the literature have no measurable effect on their performance
still beat transformers when trained on a comparable amount of data

extensive hyperparameter optimisation can give baseline models of generative adversarial networks [38], deep reinforcement learning [39] and Bayesian deep neural nets [40] the performance of more advanced proposals
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the question Does my quantum model beat classical machine learning is impossible to answer by a numerical experiment, whereas a question of clearly defined scope, such as whether the performance of a model on a specific task increases if the data or training conditions change, might be answerable.
quotes: “Does my quantum model beat classical machine learning?” is impossible to answer by a numerical experiment
“Does the performance of a model on a specific task increase as measured by some metric, if we change the data, or training conditions?” might be.
assertions.certainty_reason: A methodological position of the authors.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's own headline finding that classical models outperform the quantum ones answers a form of the first question for its setting, so the two statements need reading together.

assertions.value: The authors report an analysis of 15 randomly selected papers (out of 46 identified) using MNIST for supervised quantum machine learning benchmarks: more than half use a pre-processing strategy such as resolution reduction or PCA, only four use the original multi-class MNIST problem, and reported accuracies range from 70 to 99.6%.
quotes: a representative analysis of 15 randomly selected papers in quantum machine learning using MNIST benchmarks7 shows that more than half use a pre-processing strategy like resolution reduction or PCA to lower the number of input features
only four of the papers in our representative sample of 15 use the original MNIST multi-class problem
range from accuracies of 70 − 99.6% are mixed and hard to interpret with respect to the known baseline
These were sampled out of 46 papers that we identified to use MNIST for supervised learning benchmarks
assertions.certainty_reason: A literature sample of one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the 2-dimensional PCA-reduced MNIST 3-5 classification problem consists of about 10, 000 datapoints that lie in overlapping blobs, a task that is hardly meaningful, and that downscaling the 784 original pixels to tens of features voids the extensive knowledge about the baseline to beat; they cite Bausch for reducing images to a 4 × 4 resolution leading to 70% of test images also being present during training.
quotes: downscaling the 784 original pixels by that much voids our extensive knowledge about the baseline to beat
the 2-dimensional PCA-reduced MNIST 3-5 classification problem consists of about 10, 000 datapoints that lie in overlapping blobs
as Bausch [47] remarks, reducing images to a 4 × 4 resolution leads to 70% of test images also being present during training
assertions.certainty_reason: An author argument; the Bausch figure is a cited result.

assertions.value: The authors state that the sampled MNIST results collectively do not give convincing evidence for quantum models to systematically reach the test accuracies of 98.6% or even 99.4% put forward by Hinton for the original MNIST task, at least not if unaided by powerful classical models.
quotes: Collectively, they certainly do not give convincing evidence for quantum models to systematically reach the test accuracies of 98.6% or even 99.4% put forward by Hinton with respect to the original MNIST task
assertions.certainty_reason: An author judgment about a literature sample.

assertions.value: The paper quotes Hinton that sensibly-engineered convolutional neural nets with a few hidden layers typically get about 0.6% test error on MNIST, and that feed-forward networks with ReLUs in the permutation-invariant version typically get about 1.4% test error, reducible to around 1.1% with regularizers.
quotes: Sensibly-engineered convolutional neural nets with a few hidden layers typically get about 0.6% test error.
feed-forward neural networks with a few fully connected hidden layers of Rectified Linear Units (ReLUs) typically get about 1.4% test error.
This can be reduced to around 1.1% test error using a variety of regularizers
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Hinton.

assertions.value: The authors state that their arguments put into question the practice of adopting datasets from classical machine learning blindly when their benefits are lost, and that alternatives such as 1-d MNIST may be a lot more suitable; they still add MNIST as a task for comparability with other studies.
quotes: put into question the practice of adopting datasets from classical machine learning blindly when their benefits are lost
Alternatives, such as 1-d MNIST [48] designed to scale down deep learning experiments, may be a lot more suitable.
we will still add MNIST as a task here in order to make our results easier to compare with so many other studies
assertions.certainty_reason: An author position.

assertions.value: The authors state that they selected models in four steps: arXiv quant-ph papers from 1 January 2018 to 1 June 2023 with keywords classif*, learn*, supervised, MNIST (3500 papers); papers with 30 or more Google Scholar citations on 2 June 2023 (561 papers); papers proposing a new quantum model for classification on conventional classical data judged from the abstract (29 papers); a random subset of 15 papers of which four could not reasonably be implemented (11 papers).

to find the overwhelming share of papers that are part of the current quantum machine learning discourse. [3500 papers]

It inevitably also biases towards older papers (see Figure 4). [561 papers]

we sampled a random subset of 15 papers from the 29 candidates.

Selecting papers with 30 or more citations introduces a bias towards less recent work.

assertions.value: The authors state that from the final selection of 11 papers they implemented 12 quantum machine learning models, because Havlicek et al. compared two distinct architectures, both of which they implemented, and that the 12 models split into three families: quantum neural networks, quantum kernel methods and quantum convolutional neural networks.

both of which we implemented.

assertions.value: The authors state that they study six quantum neural network classifiers and then describe CircuitCentricClassifier, DataReuploadingClassifier, DressedQuantumCircuitClassifier, IQPVariationalClassifier, QuantumBoltzmannMachine, QuantumMetricLearner and TreeTensorClassifier.
quotes: We study six quantum neural network classifiers:

The choice of loss function for training varies among models9. Two models use a cross entropy loss, three use a square loss, one uses a linear loss, and one uses a loss based on distances between embedded quantum states
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own count disagrees with its own list.
assertions.reader_inference: The list names seven models, and the loss counts (two, three, one, one) also sum to seven. Seven QNNs plus three kernel methods plus two convolutional models give the stated 12 models, so six appears to be a typo for seven.

assertions.value: The authors define a quantum neural network model as one that combines one or more variational quantum circuits, each of the form f(theta, x) = tr[O(x, theta) rho(x, theta)], to classify data into one of two labels y = ±1 through a class prediction function, and note that quantum neural networks are simply variational quantum circuits that encode data and are trainable by gradient-descent methods.
quotes: simply variational quantum circuits that encode data and are trainable by gradientdescent methods

For our purposes, a quantum neural network model is one that combines one or more such variational quantum circuits {f1, ..., fL} to classify data into one of two labels y = ±1 through a class prediction function fpred:
assertions.certainty_reason: A definition stated by the paper in Section II.B.1.

assertions.value: The authors define a quantum kernel method as one in which the kernel function is evaluated with the aid of a quantum computer, commonly by embedding the classical data into quantum states rho(x) and using the kernel k(xi, xj) = tr[rho(xi) rho(xj)].
quotes: A quantum kernel method is one in which the kernel function is evaluated with the aid of a quantum computer.
which is a kernel by virtue of being an inner product, and can be evaluated by methods that evaluate state overlaps.
assertions.certainty_reason: A definition stated by the paper in Section II.B.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not capture quantum convolutional models in a strict mathematical definition but identify them as quantum neural network models that, like classical convolutional models, exploit a form of translation symmetry, and that they study two such models, QuanvolutionalNeuralNetwork and WeiNet.

assertions.value: The authors state in Section II.B that QuantumKitchenSinks is loosely included among the quantum kernel methods and that its implementation does use a SVM as in the other two models, and state in Appendix C that the feature mapped vectors are passed to a linear classifier implemented using scikit-learn’s LogisticRegression class.

assertions.value: The authors state three principles for dataset choice: predominantly artificially generated data to vary properties and size, maximal diversity of datasets through fundamentally different generators, and, in the last three of six data generation procedures, the manifold hypothesis that typical data effectively lives on low-dimensional manifolds; they do not claim to answer which data suits quantum models.
quotes: We followed three overarching principles: Firstly, we predominantly use artificially generated data which allows us to understand and vary the properties and size of the datasets.
Secondly, we aim at maximising the diversity of the datasets by using fundamentally different functional relationships and procedures as generators
Thirdly, in the last three out of six data generation procedures introduced below we follow the “manifold hypothesis” [74–76]

quotes: Then any minimum norm point in C is Pareto optimal, corresponding to the other endpoint of the trade-off curve.
If both norms are Euclidean, this Pareto optimal point is unique, and given by x = A†b, where A† is the pseudoinverse of A.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that regularization is a scalarization method for the bi-criterion problem: minimizing the weighted sum of norms with gamma positive traces out the optimal trade-off curve, and the weighted sum of squared norms is another form; it is interpreted as prior knowledge that x is not large, a cost on large design variables, a model validity safeguard, and a compromise for poorly conditioned or singular square systems.
quotes: As γ varies over (0, ∞), the solution of (6.8) traces out the optimal trade-off curve.
In cases where A is poorly conditioned, or even singular, regularization gives a compromise between solving the equations (i.e., making Ax − b zero) and keeping x of reasonable size.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book defines Tikhonov regularization as minimizing the squared Euclidean residual plus delta times the squared norm of x, a convex quadratic problem with the analytical solution (A transpose A plus delta I) inverse A transpose b, valid without rank assumptions since A transpose A plus delta I is positive definite for positive delta.
quotes: Since AT A + δI ≻ 0 for any δ > 0, the Tikhonov regularized least-squares solution requires no rank (or dimension) assumptions on the matrix A.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that regularization can use a term of the form norm of D x in place of norm of x, with D an approximate differentiation operator so that D x measures variation or smoothness, for example a second-difference matrix whose squared norm measures mean-square curvature, and that terms for smoothness and size can be combined.
quotes: In many applications, the matrix D represents an approximate differentiation or second-order differentiation operator, so Dx represents a measure of the variation or smoothness of x.
We can also add several regularization terms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book reports an illustrative optimal input design example (impulse response of a decaying system, input sequence of length N plus one with N equal 200) minimizing tracking error plus delta times input variation plus eta times input magnitude: with small magnitude regularization the tracking is good but the input is large and rapidly varying; more magnitude regularization gives a smaller input at the cost of larger tracking error; adding variation regularization substantially reduces input variation with not much increase in tracking error.
quotes: Now we consider a specific example, with N = 200, and impulse response
While the tracking is good (i.e., we have Jtrack is small), the input required is large, and rapidly varying.
The input variation is substantially reduced, with not much increase in output tracking error.
assertions.reader_inference: One constructed example with chosen parameters, not a study.

assertions.value: The book states that varying gamma in the problem minimize the Euclidean residual plus gamma times the l1-norm of x sweeps out a trade-off curve that serves as an approximation of the trade-off between the residual and the cardinality card(x) of x, and that the problem can be recast and solved as an SOCP.
quotes: which serves as an approximation of the optimal trade-off curve between Ax − b 2 and the sparsity or cardinality card(x) of the vector x
The problem (6.11) can be recast and solved as an SOCP.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that choosing k of n regressors (minimize the residual norm subject to card(x) at most k) is in general a hard combinatorial problem, solved exactly by enumerating all n choose k sparsity patterns with least-squares each, and that a good heuristic is to solve the l1-regularized problem for different gamma, take the smallest gamma giving card(x) equal k, fix that sparsity pattern and re-solve by least squares.
quotes: In general, this is a hard combinatorial problem.
A good heuristic approach is to solve the problem (6.11) for different values of γ, finding the smallest value of γ that results in a solution with card(x) = k.

assertions.value: The book reports a numerical example of the regressor selection heuristic with A of 10 rows and 20 columns, comparing the globally Pareto optimal values (by enumerating all sparsity patterns) with the l1 heuristic values, noting the heuristic finds the global optimum for card(x) equal one.
quotes: Figure 6.7 illustrates a numerical example with A ∈ R10×20, x ∈ R20, b ∈ R10.
For each k, the Pareto optimal point was obtained by enumerating all possible sparsity patterns with k nonzero entries, as described above.

assertions.value: The book defines the signal reconstruction (de-noising, smoothing) problem as the convex bi-criterion problem minimizing (the l2 distance of the estimate from the corrupted signal, phi of the estimate), with phi a convex smoothing objective measuring roughness, solved for Pareto optimal points by scalarization.
quotes: The function φ : Rn → R is convex, and is called the regularization function or smoothing objective.
The reconstruction problem (6.12) is a convex bi-criterion problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book defines quadratic smoothing as the sum of squared successive differences, equal to the squared norm of D x, and states the minimizer of the squared distance plus delta times that is x-hat equal (I plus delta D transpose D) inverse x_cor, computable very efficiently since the matrix is tridiagonal.
quotes: The solution of this quadratic problem, xˆ = (I + δDT D)−1xcor, can be computed very efficiently since I + δDT D is tridiagonal; see appendix C.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book reports a quadratic smoothing example with a signal of 4000 samples: the optimal trade-off curve has a clear knee near a residual distance of about 3, the left extreme (estimate equals the corrupted signal) has norm of D x_cor equal 4.4, the right extreme (estimate zero) has distance 16.2, and the best reconstruction is at the knee, with too much smoothing at higher distances and too little at lower.
quotes: Figure 6.8 shows a signal x ∈ R4000 (top) and the corrupted signal xcor (bottom).
has objective value Dxcor 2 = 4.4.
for which xˆ − xcor 2 = xcor 2 = 16.2.
Note the clear knee in the trade-off curve near xˆ − xcor 2 ≈ 3.
Comparing the reconstructed signals with the original signal x, we see that the best reconstruction is obtained for xˆ − xcor 2 = 3, which corresponds to the knee of the trade-off curve.
assertions.reader_inference: One synthetic signal; the authors read the best reconstruction by eye from plots.

assertions.value: The book defines the total variation smoothing function as the sum of absolute successive differences (the l1 norm of D x-hat), which assigns relatively less penalty to large jumps than quadratic smoothing, and reports on a signal with jumps that quadratic smoothing also smooths out the rapid variations while total variation reconstruction preserves the sharp transitions.
quotes: The total variation measure, however, assigns relatively less penalty to large values of |xi+1 − xi|.
We observe that, unlike quadratic smoothing, total variation reconstruction preserves the sharp transitions in the signal.
assertions.reader_inference: One synthetic example illustrated with plots; the figure values are not in the text.

assertions.value: The book states in a caption that in total variation reconstruction the sharp changes in the signal are preserved, unlike quadratic smoothing, and that the smoothest of the three displayed reconstructions does not give quite enough noise reduction while the other eliminates some slowly varying parts of the signal.
quotes: Note that in total variation reconstruction, unlike quadratic smoothing, the sharp changes in the signal are preserved.
assertions.reader_inference: Read from plots of one synthetic example.

assertions.value: The book defines the stochastic robust approximation problem as minimizing the expected norm of A x minus b for random A equal to a mean matrix plus zero-mean U, states it is always convex but usually intractable, and that it is tractable when A takes finitely many values: the sum-of-norms problem, an SOCP for the Euclidean norm and an LP for the l1 or l-infinity norm.
quotes: It is always a convex optimization problem, but usually not tractable since in most cases it is very difficult to evaluate the objective or its derivatives.
If the norm is the Euclidean norm, this sum-of-norms problem is an SOCP.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book derives that the stochastic robust least-squares problem (expected squared residual) has the form of a regularized least-squares problem with the matrix P equal to the expectation of U transpose U and solution (A-bar transpose A-bar plus P) inverse A-bar transpose b, and interprets Tikhonov regularization as a robust least-squares problem for uncorrelated zero-mean perturbations with variance delta over m.
quotes: with solution x = (A ̄T A ̄ + P )−1A ̄T b.
The solution of the Tikhonov regularized leastsquares problem (6.10) minimizes E (A + U )x − b 2, where Uij are zero mean, uncorrelated random variables, with variance δ/m
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book defines the worst-case robust approximation problem as minimizing the supremum of the norm of A x minus b over a nonempty bounded set of possible matrices; the worst-case error is always convex in x, the problem is always convex, but tractability depends on the norm and the uncertainty set.
quotes: which is always a convex function of x.
The robust approximation problem is always a convex optimization problem, but its tractability depends on the norm used and the description of the uncertainty set A.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book reports a constructed example with A(u) equal A0 plus u A1 (variation in the matrix roughly plus or minus ten percent) in which the nominal solution has the smallest residual at u equal zero but much larger residuals as u approaches the ends of the interval, the worst-case solution has a larger residual at zero but residuals that do not rise much over the interval, and the stochastic robust solution is in between.
quotes: The nominal solution achieves the smallest residual when u = 0, but is quite sensitive to parameter variation
The stochastic robust approximate solution is in between.
assertions.reader_inference: A single constructed instance, not a study.

assertions.value: The book calls noise added to the measurement additive error and variation in A multiplicative error, interprets the robust problem as robust design, and states that for a finite set of matrices the worst-case problem is equivalent to using the polyhedral set conv{A_1, ..., A_k}, solvable as an SOCP (Euclidean norm) or LP (l1 or l-infinity norm).
quotes: In contrast, the variation in A is called multiplicative error, since it multiplies the variable x.
This problem is equivalent to the robust approximation problem with the polyhedral set A = conv{A1, . . . , Ak}
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book derives that for a spectral-norm ball of uncertainty of radius a, the worst-case error is the norm of A-bar x minus b plus a times the norm of x, so the robust problem is a regularized norm problem solvable as an SOCP, and its solution coincides with that of the regularized least-squares problem for some delta, giving another interpretation of regularized least-squares as worst-case robust approximation.
quotes: for some value of the regularization parameter δ, we have another interpretation of the regularized least-squares problem as a worst-case robust approximation problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that with ellipsoidal uncertainty in each row, the worst-case magnitude of each residual is the nominal residual magnitude plus the norm of P_i transpose x, so the robust l2-norm approximation problem reduces to an SOCP.
quotes: = |a ̄iT x − bi| + PiT x 2.
can be reduced to an SOCP, as follows.

assertions.value: The book states that for uncertainty given as the image of an infinity-norm ball under an affine map, the worst-case error of the robust Chebyshev approximation problem is the maximum over i of the l1 norm of the ith row of P(x) plus the absolute value of q_i(x), so the problem can be cast as an LP.
quotes: The robust Chebyshev approximation problem can therefore be cast as an LP
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book derives that the worst-case error for Euclidean-norm-bounded structured uncertainty is the square root of the optimal value of a nonconvex quadratic maximization over the unit ball, whose Lagrange dual is an SDP and for which strong duality holds (as discussed in Section 5.2 and proved in the appendix), so the robust least-squares problem is equivalent to the SDP in x, lambda and t.
quotes: Moreover, as mentioned in §5.2 and §B.1 (and proved in §B.4), strong duality holds for this pair of primal and dual problems.
We conclude that the robust least-squares problem is equivalent to the SDP (6.15) with x, λ, t as variables.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book reports on one constructed instance (m equal 50, n equal 20, a large nominal matrix and perturbation matrices about ten percent of its norm) evaluated on a large number of random parameter vectors in the unit disk that the nominal least-squares residuals range from about 0.52 to 4.9, whereas the robust least-squares solution has a residual between 2.0 and 2.6 for all parameters, with Tikhonov regularized (delta equal one) similar in spread.
quotes: First, the residuals of the nominal least-squares solution are widely spread, from a smallest value around 0.52 to a largest value around 4.9.
The robust least-squares solution, for example, achieves a residual between 2.0 and 2.6 for all parameters in the unit disk.
with dimensions m = 50, n = 20.

assertions.value: The book defines the function fitting problem as choosing a member of a finite-dimensional subspace spanned by basis functions f_1, ..., f_n with coefficient vector x, with polynomials, trigonometric polynomials and piecewise-linear functions on a triangulated domain as example families.
quotes: In function fitting problems, we select a member of a finite-dimensional subspace of functions that best fits some given data or requirements.
The family {f1, . . . , fn} is sometimes called the set of basis functions (for the fitting problem) even when the functions are not independent.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that a piecewise-affine function on a triangulated domain is built by assigning function values to grid points and extending affinely on each simplex, with basis functions equal to one at their own grid point and zero at the others, so it is continuous; piecewise polynomials with continuous derivatives up to some order define spline classes, and a cubic spline with three pieces on a line has dimension six (twelve coefficients with six equality constraints).
quotes: By construction, such a function is continuous.
In this example, the dimension of the family of functions is n = 6, since we have 12 polynomial coefficients (4 per cubic polynomial), and 6 equality constraints (3 each at u1 and u2).
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that value interpolation conditions, function value inequalities and Lipschitz constraints at a finite set of points are linear in the coefficient vector x, that nonnegativity at infinitely many points is a convex constraint (an intersection of infinitely many halfspaces) tractable only in special cases such as piecewise-linear functions or polynomials, and that derivative constraints are linear equalities, convex gradient-norm bounds or LMIs.
quotes: Therefore interpolation conditions f (vj) = zj, j = 1, . . . , m, which require the function f to have the values zj ∈ R at specified points vj ∈ D, form a set of linear equalities in x.
This is a convex constraint on x (since it is the intersection of an infinite number of halfspaces), but may not lead to a tractable problem except in special cases

assertions.value: The book states that requiring f to be monotone or convex over all points is a convex constraint on x but may not be tractable except in special cases: for piecewise-affine f monotonicity is a finite set of linear inequalities, and for quadratic f convexity reduces to the quadratic part being positive semidefinite, an LMI.
quotes: When f is piecewise affine, for example, the monotonicity constraint is equivalent to the condition ∇f (v) 0 inside each of the simplexes.
the convexity constraint reduces to the requirement that the quadratic part of f be nonnegative, which is an LMI.

assertions.value: The book states that any linear functional L on the subspace of functions is a linear function of x, so a constraint L(f) equal a, such as a moment constraint, is a linear equality constraint on x.

assertions.value: The book states that least-squares fitting of a function in a finite-dimensional subspace is a least-squares problem in x, that polynomial fitting is a norm approximation problem with a Vandermonde-type matrix, and reports a polynomial fitting example with 40 data points and polynomials of maximum degree five for the l2 and l-infinity norms.
quotes: which is a simple least-squares problem in the variable x.
Figure 6.19 shows an example with m = 40 data points and n = 6 (i.e., polynomials of maximum degree 5), for the l2- and l∞-norms.

assertions.value: The book reports a spline fitting example with the same data as the polynomial example: the interval is divided into three equal intervals and cubic splines with continuous first and second derivatives form a subspace of dimension six, the same as degree five polynomials; with many more data points than the dimension, smoothing is automatic since all members of the subspace are smooth.
quotes: The dimension of this subspace of functions is 6, the same as the dimension of polynomials with maximum degree 5, considered in example 6.7.
Smoothing is accomplished automatically, since all members of the subspace are smooth.

assertions.value: The book states that with fewer data points than the dimension of the subspace, interpolation conditions are linear equalities and the smoothest or smallest interpolating function solves a least-norm problem; the fit gives interpolation or extrapolation at new points, an interval for f(v) can be produced by maximizing and minimizing it subject to the constraints, and an l1-norm fit can help identify outliers.
quotes: Among the functions that satisfy these interpolation conditions, we might seek one that is smoothest, or smallest. These lead to least-norm problems.
We can also produce an interval in which the value f (v) can lie, by maximizing and minimizing (the linear function) f (v), subject to the constraints.

assertions.value: The book defines basis pursuit as fitting data by a linear combination of a small number of basis functions chosen from a very large, linearly dependent dictionary (over-complete basis) with a sparse coefficient vector, states it is mathematically the same as regressor selection, and lists uses in de-noising and data compression.
quotes: In basis pursuit, there is a very large number of basis functions, and the goal is to find a good fit of the given data as a linear combination of a small number of the basis functions.
Mathematically, basis pursuit is the same as the regressor selection problem (see §6.4), but the interpretation (and scale) of the optimization problem are different.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book describes the basis pursuit procedure: solve the l1-regularized least-squares problem with parameter gamma, take the nonzero coefficient pattern, then solve a least-squares problem restricted to those basis elements; it notes dictionaries can have n on the order of ten thousand or more so algorithms must exploit structure.
quotes: The solution of this problem can be used directly, or followed by a refinement step, in which the best fit is found, using the sparsity pattern of the solution of (6.18).
To be effective, algorithms for solving (6.18) must exploit problem structure
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

so all together there are 501 × 61 = 30561 basis elements.
we can interpret this as meaning that the data contains the frequency ω at time τ .

assertions.value: The book proves the convex interpolation criterion: given a convex f with domain all of R^k, subgradients g_i exist at each point (the gradient if differentiable, otherwise from a supporting hyperplane to the epigraph) and applying the affine underestimator at the other points gives the inequalities; conversely given g_i satisfying the inequalities, the maximum of the affine functions y_i plus g_i transpose (z minus u_i) is a piecewise-linear convex function interpolating the data.
quotes: In some special cases we can solve interpolation problems involving an infinitedimensional set of functions, using finite-dimensional convex optimization.
Clearly, f is a (piecewise-linear) convex function. The inequalities (6.19) imply that f (ui) = yi, for i = 1, . . . , m.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that the optimal value of the QP for least-squares fitting of a convex function is zero if and only if the data can be interpolated by a convex function, and that the problem as posed has an infinite-dimensional variable, the function itself.
quotes: The optimal value of this problem is zero if and only if the given data can be interpolated by a convex function

assertions.value: The book states that, for data that can be interpolated by a convex function, the smallest possible value of f at another point u0 over all interpolating convex functions is the optimal value of an LP in y0 and the subgradients, and maximizing y0 gives the largest possible value.
quotes: By maximizing y0 (which is also an LP) we find the largest possible value of f (u0) for a convex function that interpolates the given data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book models a consumer's preferences by an underlying utility function that is monotone nondecreasing (more of any good is preferred) and concave (satiation), and states that consistency of strict and weak preference data with some concave nondecreasing utility function is an infinite-dimensional feasibility problem equivalent to a finite LP feasibility problem in the utilities and subgradients, using the monotone convex interpolation result.
quotes: It is reasonable to assume that u is monotone nondecreasing.
It is also reasonable to assume that u is concave. This models satiation, or decreasing marginal utility as we increase the amount of goods.
This problem, in turn, can be cast as a (finite-dimensional) linear programming feasibility problem, using the interpolation result on page 339
assertions.certainty_reason: The book states its own scope at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that if the LP is feasible there is at least one consistent concave nondecreasing utility function (constructible piecewise-linear), if infeasible none exists, and that an unknown preference between baskets k and l can sometimes be concluded by adding the opposite weak preference and checking infeasibility, in which case basket k is definitely preferred without knowing the utility function.
quotes: If (6.25) is not feasible, we can conclude that there is no concave increasing utility function that is consistent with the given sets of strict and nonstrict preferences.
In other words, we can conclude that basket k is preferred to basket l, without knowing the underlying utility function.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book reports a numerical example with forty random baskets of two goods compared to the basket (0.5, 0.5): 21 baskets are definitely rejected in favor of it, 14 are definitely preferred, and no conclusion is possible for the remaining 5, with monotonicity alone settling 17 of the baskets and concavity plus the feasibility LP needed for the 23 in the other two quadrants.
quotes: We find that 21 of the baskets are definitely rejected in favor of (0.5, 0.5), and 14 of the baskets are definitely preferred. We cannot make any conclusion, from the consumer preference data, about the remaining 5 baskets.
So for these 17 points, there is no need to solve the feasibility LP (6.25).
Classifying the 23 points in the other two quadrants, however, requires the concavity assumption, and solving the feasibility LP (6.25).
assertions.reader_inference: One synthetic example with a known utility function used to generate the preferences; not a study of real consumers.

assertions.value: The authors attribute the robustness analysis of penalty functions and the Huber penalty to Huber, state that Tikhonov regularization is sometimes called ridge regression, that least-squares approximation with l1-norm regularization is known as lasso (Tibshirani), that total variation denoising was introduced for image reconstruction by Rudin, Osher and Fatemi, and that Chen, Donoho and Saunders call the l1-regularized problem basis pursuit denoising.
quotes: Tikhonov regularization is sometimes called ridge regression
Least-squares approximation with l1-norm regularization is also known under the name lasso

assertions.value: The book states, as exercises, that a monotone nondecreasing interpolant exists if and only if y_i is at least y_j whenever u_i is componentwise at least u_j, and that a quasiconvex interpolant exists if and only if there exist g_i with g_i transpose (u_j minus u_i) at most minus one whenever y_j is less than y_i.
quotes: Show that there exists a quasiconvex function f : Rk → R, that satisfies f (ui) = yi for i = 1, . . . , m, if and only if there exist gi ∈ Rk, i = 1, . . . , m, such that giT (uj − ui) ≤ −1 whenever yj < yi, i, j = 1, . . . , m.

assertions.value: The book states, as an exercise citing the Riesz-Fejer theorem, that the set of vectors interpolable by a positive-real function is a closed convex cone described by positive semidefiniteness of the Nevanlinna-Pick matrix, so least-squares fitting by a positive-real function is a convex problem.
quotes: The matrix P (y) is called the Nevanlinna-Pick matrix associated with the points zk, yk.
Use the following result (known as Riesz-Fej ́er theorem; see [KN77, page 60]).

assertions.value: The book defines the likelihood function of a parametrized family of densities for a fixed observed sample, its logarithm the log-likelihood, and maximum likelihood estimation as choosing the parameter that maximizes the likelihood, with prior information as constraints (or likelihood zero outside the constraint set).
quotes: A widely used method, called maximum likelihood (ML) estimation, is to estimate x as xˆml = argmaxxpx(y) = argmaxxl(x)
When considered as a function of x, for fixed y ∈ Rm, the function px(y) is called the likelihood function.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that the ML problem is convex if the log-likelihood is concave for each observation and the constraint set is described by linear equalities and convex inequalities, which occurs in many estimation problems, so an ML estimate can then be computed by convex optimization.
quotes: a situation which occurs in many estimation problems. For these problems we can compute an ML estimate using convex optimization.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that for linear measurements with IID noise of density p, the ML estimate maximizes the sum of log p(y_i minus a_i transpose x), a convex problem when p is log-concave and of the form of a penalty approximation problem with penalty minus log p.
quotes: If the density p is log-concave, this problem is convex, and has the form of a penalty approximation problem
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that Gaussian noise gives the ML estimate as the least-squares solution, Laplacian noise gives the l1-norm approximation, and uniform noise on an interval gives any x with the infinity-norm residual at most the interval half-width.
quotes: Therefore the ML estimate of x is xml = argminx Ax − y 2 2 , the solution of a least-squares approximation problem.
and an ML estimate is any x satisfying Ax − y ∞ ≤ a.

assertions.value: The book states that any penalty function approximation problem can be interpreted as ML estimation with noise density p(z) proportional to e to the minus phi(z); rapidly growing penalties correspond to light-tailed noise, and l1-norm approximation is ML with Laplacian noise, whose larger tails than the Gaussian explain its robustness to large errors.
quotes: We interpret l1-norm approximation as maximum likelihood estimation with a noise density that is Laplacian; l2-norm approximation is maximum likelihood estimation with a Gaussian noise density.

quotes: For x ∈ dom f , the vector ∆xnt = −∇2f (x)−1∇f (x) is called the Newton step (for f , at x).
so the Newton step is a descent direction (unless x is optimal).
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book gives interpretations of the Newton step: it minimizes the second-order Taylor approximation (exact for a quadratic f, intuitively very good near the optimum); it is the steepest descent direction in the quadratic norm defined by the Hessian, with P equal to the Hessian at the optimum a very good choice near x-star; and it solves the linearized optimality condition, in one variable the zero crossing of the linearized derivative.
quotes: Thus, the Newton step ∆xnt is what should be added to the point x to minimize the second-order approximation of f at x.
The Newton step is also the steepest descent direction at x, for the quadratic norm defined by the Hessian ∇2f (x)
So the Newton step ∆xnt is what must be added to x so that the linearized optimality condition holds.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book proves the Newton step is independent of linear or affine changes of coordinates: for f-bar(y) equal f(T y) with T nonsingular the gradient and Hessian transform by T transpose, so the Newton step for f-bar at y is T inverse times the Newton step of f at x.
quotes: Hence the Newton steps of f and f ̄ are related by the same linear transformation, and x + ∆xnt = T (y + ∆ynt).
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book defines the Newton decrement at x as the square root of the gradient transpose times the inverse Hessian times the gradient, and states it plays an important role in the analysis of Newton's method and is useful as a stopping criterion.
quotes: The quantity λ(x) = ∇f (x)T ∇2f (x)−1∇f (x) 1/2 is called the Newton decrement at x.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that half the squared Newton decrement equals f(x) minus the minimum of the second-order approximation, so it estimates f(x) minus p-star, that the decrement is the norm of the Newton step in the Hessian norm, that the gradient transpose times the Newton step equals minus the squared decrement (the constant in backtracking line search), and that the decrement is, like the step, affine invariant.
quotes: Thus, λ2/2 is an estimate of f (x) − p⋆, based on the quadratic approximation of f at x.
Finally, we note that the Newton decrement is, like the Newton step, affine invariant.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states Newton's method (damped or guarded Newton, to distinguish it from the pure Newton method with fixed unit step): compute the Newton step and decrement, stop if half the squared decrement is at most epsilon, choose the step by backtracking line search, update; it is the general descent method with the Newton step as direction and the stopping criterion checked after computing the direction.
quotes: Newton's method, as outlined below, is sometimes called the damped Newton method or guarded Newton method, to distinguish it from the pure Newton method, which uses a fixed step size t = 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book assumes for the convergence analysis that f is twice continuously differentiable, strongly convex with constant m (so a bound M exists) and has a Hessian Lipschitz continuous on S with constant L, which measures how well f is approximated by a quadratic model (zero for quadratics); intuition suggests Newton's method works well when L is small.
quotes: In addition, we assume that the Hessian of f is Lipschitz continuous on S with constant L, i.e.,
The coefficient L, which can be interpreted as a bound on the third derivative of f , can be taken to be zero for a quadratic function.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book states its own scope at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book proves that there exist numbers eta (at most m squared over L) and gamma (positive) such that if the gradient norm is at least eta then the objective decreases by at least gamma, and if the gradient norm is below eta the backtracking line search takes the full step t equal one and the gradient norm contracts quadratically; once the second condition holds it holds for all later iterates.
quotes: Continuing recursively, we conclude that once the second condition holds, it will hold for all future iterates
This last inequality shows that convergence is extremely rapid once the second condition is satisfied.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that once the pure Newton phase is reached convergence is quadratic (roughly, the number of correct digits doubles each iteration), that the number of damped phase iterations is at most (f(x0) minus p-star) over gamma, and that the quadratic phase needs at most a doubly logarithmic number of iterations in the accuracy, so the total number of iterations is bounded by the sum and, treating the slowly growing second term as about six, by (f(x0) minus p-star) over gamma plus six.
quotes: This phenomenon is called quadratic convergence.
Overall, then, the number of iterations until f (x) − p⋆ ≤ ǫ is bounded above by

quotes: Therefore the line search returns a step size t ≥ βm/M , resulting in a decrease of the objective function
Therefore, (9.32) is satisfied with γ = αβη2 m M2 . (9.38)

assertions.value: The book proves the quadratically convergent phase: the backtracking search accepts unit steps when the gradient norm is small enough relative to m squared over L (using the Lipschitz Hessian condition and integrating the second derivative bound), and the Lipschitz condition then bounds the new gradient norm by a constant times the squared old gradient norm.
quotes: which shows that the unit step t = 1 is accepted by the backtracking line search.
i.e., the inequality (9.33).

assertions.value: The book reports for Newton's method with backtracking (alpha 0.1, beta 0.7) on the two-variable test function that convergence to a very high accuracy is achieved in only five iterations, with quadratic convergence clearly apparent: the last step reduces the error from about 10 to the minus 5 to about 10 to the minus 10.

Newton's method with backtracking line search on the test function (9.20), with line search parameters α = 0.1, β = 0.7.

assertions.value: The book reports for the earlier barrier problem that Newton's method with backtracking attains very high accuracy in eight iterations with quadratic convergence evident after about the third iteration, that exact line search saves only one iteration, that the backtracking parameters have little effect (with alpha fixed at 0.01 and beta between 0.2 and 1 the iteration count varies between 8 and 12), and that practical implementations use a small alpha such as 0.01 and a larger beta such as 0.5.

With α fixed at 0.01, and values of β varying between 0.2 and 1, the number of iterations required varies between 8 and 12.
most practical implementations use a backtracking line search with a small value of α, such as 0.01, and a larger value of β, such as 0.5.

assertions.value: The book reports a large-scale example (a log barrier objective with m equal 100000 and n equal 10000 and random sparse data) where Newton's method with backtracking shows a linearly convergent initial phase of about 13 iterations then 4 or 5 more quadratically convergent iterations to very high accuracy, 18 iterations in total.

assertions.value: The book states that Newton's method is independent of affine changes of coordinates: applying it (with the same backtracking parameters) to f(T y) from y0 equal T inverse x0 gives iterates with T y_k equal x_k and the same stopping criterion, in contrast to the gradient method; in exact arithmetic Newton's method is insensitive to condition numbers, and with finite precision very large condition numbers do not adversely affect a real implementation.
quotes: In other words, Newton's method is the same: The iterates are related by the same change of coordinates.
But we can say that condition numbers ranging up to very large values such as 1010 do not adversely affect a real implementation of Newton's method.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book reports that on the family of scaled problems for which the gradient method slows to useless for extreme gamma, Newton's method solves the problem in nine iterations for a huge range of gamma, so choice of coordinates is a first-order issue for gradient methods and a second-order issue for Newton's method.
quotes: In contrast, Newton's method (with α = 0.01, β = 0.5) solves this problem (in fact, to a far higher accuracy) in nine iterations, for all values of γ between 10−10 and 1010.
While choice of coordinates (or condition number of sublevel sets) is a first-order issue for gradient and steepest descent methods, it is a second-order issue for Newton's method
assertions.reader_inference: One constructed family of problems.

assertions.value: The book states that Newton's method's main disadvantage is the cost of forming and storing the Hessian and solving the Newton system (often reducible by exploiting structure), and that quasi-Newton methods need less effort per direction while sharing some advantages such as rapid convergence near the optimum, but are not covered in the book.
quotes: The main disadvantage of Newton's method is the cost of forming and storing the Hessian, and the cost of computing the Newton step, which requires solving a set of linear equations.
These methods require less computational effort to form the search direction, but they share some of the strong advantages of Newton methods, such as rapid convergence near x⋆.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book states this limit at the anchor.

assertions.value: The authors state two shortcomings of the classical Newton analysis: the complexity estimates involve the three constants m, M and L, which are almost never known in practice, and the analysis depends on the coordinate system even though the method is affine invariant, since m, M and L all change with coordinates.
quotes: There are two major shortcomings of the classical convergence analysis of Newton's method given in §9.5.3.
If we change coordinates the constants m, M , and L all change.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book states this limit at the anchor.

assertions.value: The authors state that self-concordance, discovered by Nesterov and Nemirovski, is wanted because self-concordant functions include many logarithmic barrier functions of interior-point methods, the analysis of Newton's method for them involves no unknown constants, and the property is affine invariant so the complexity estimate is independent of coordinates.
quotes: The analysis of Newton's method for self-concordant functions does not depend on any unknown constants.
Self-concordance is an affine-invariant property

assertions.value: The book shows the negative logarithm is self-concordant (the defining inequality holds with equality), that linear and convex quadratic functions are self-concordant, that negative entropy plus negative logarithm is self-concordant, and that negative entropy by itself is not.
quotes: so the defining inequality (9.41) holds with equality.
The negative entropy function by itself is not self-concordant

assertions.value: The book shows that the log barrier for linear inequalities is self-concordant (each term is a negative logarithm composed with an affine map, and sums preserve self-concordance), and that minus the log of a concave quadratic is self-concordant by reduction to one variable.
quotes: Therefore the sum is also self-concordant.
which establishes self-concordance.

assertions.value: The book states, with proof left to an exercise, that if g is convex on the positive reals with the third derivative bounded by the second derivative over x, then minus log of minus g minus log x is self-concordant, and lists functions satisfying it, from which self-concordance of several barrier functions (for the second-order cone, p-norm cone and exponential cone) follows.
quotes: Then f (x) = − log(−g(x)) − log x is self-concordant on {x | x > 0, g(x) < 0}. (For a proof, see exercise 9.14.)

assertions.value: The book states that for strictly convex self-concordant functions bounds in terms of the Newton decrement are unaffected by affine changes of coordinates, that the decrement equals the supremum over directions of minus v transpose gradient over the Hessian norm of v, and that the second derivative along a line is bounded between f''(0) over (1 plus t sqrt(f''(0))) squared and f''(0) over (1 minus t sqrt(f''(0))) squared.
quotes: Unlike the bounds based on the norm of the gradient, the bounds based on the Newton decrement are not affected by an affine change of coordinates.
The lower bound is valid for all nonnegative t ∈ dom f ; the upper bound is valid if t ∈ dom f and 0 ≤ t < f ′′(0)−1/2.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book derives that for a strictly convex self-concordant function p-star is at least f(x) plus lambda(x) plus log(one minus lambda(x)) when lambda(x) is below one, and that minus (lambda plus log(one minus lambda)) is at most lambda squared for lambda at most 0.68, giving p-star at least f(x) minus lambda squared; doubling the quadratic-model estimate lambda squared over two gives a provable bound, and a stopping criterion lambda squared at most epsilon guarantees f(x) minus p-star at most epsilon.
quotes: Thus, we have the bound on suboptimality p⋆ ≥ f (x) − λ(x)2, (9.50) valid for λ(x) ≤ 0.68.
the inequality (9.50) shows that for self-concordant functions, doubling this estimate gives us a provable bound.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book proves for Newton's method with backtracking on a strictly convex self-concordant function, bounded below with closed initial sublevel set, that there exist eta (at most one quarter) and gamma depending only on the line search parameters such that if the decrement exceeds eta the objective decreases by at least gamma, and if it is at most eta the unit step is chosen and the decrement contracts quadratically (two times the new decrement is at most the square of two times the old), giving a damped phase of at most (f(x0) minus p-star) over gamma steps and a quadratic phase of at most a doubly logarithmic number of steps.

assertions.value: The book defines the Newton step at a feasible point as the solution of the equality constrained quadratic minimization of the second-order Taylor approximation, characterized by a KKT system in the Hessian and A, defined only where that KKT matrix is nonsingular, and equal to the solution of the linearized optimality conditions.
quotes: We define ∆xnt, the Newton step at x, as the solution of the convex quadratic problem (10.10), assuming the associated KKT matrix is nonsingular.

assertions.value: The book states that when the objective is exactly quadratic the Newton update solves the equality constrained problem exactly and the vector w is the optimal dual variable of the original problem.

assertions.value: The book defines the Newton decrement for the equality constrained problem as the square root of the step times the Hessian times the step, and states that f(x) minus the minimum of the second-order model over the feasible set equals half the decrement squared, so half the decrement squared estimates f(x) minus p-star and serves as a stopping criterion; the directional derivative along the step is minus the decrement squared.

assertions.value: The book states that the equality constrained Newton step is always a feasible descent direction, except when x is optimal and the step is zero: A times the step is zero, and descent follows from the directional derivative being minus the decrement squared.

assertions.value: The book shows that the Newton step and decrement for equality constrained minimization are affine invariant: under a nonsingular change of variables x equals T y, the step at y satisfies T times the step at y equals the step at x, with the same dual vector w.

assertions.value: The book gives an algorithm for equality constrained Newton: from a feasible start, compute the step and decrement, stop when the decrement squared over two is at most epsilon, backtrack, update; it is a feasible descent method in which every iterate is feasible and the objective decreases, and it requires the KKT matrix to be invertible at each point.

assertions.value: The book defines the Newton step at a point that need not be feasible by linearizing the optimality conditions, giving a linear system whose right-hand side contains the residual A x minus b; it reduces to the feasible Newton step when x is feasible.

assertions.value: The book shows that a damped step of length t scales the primal residual down by the factor one minus t, so after k steps the residual equals the product of those factors times the initial residual, always in the direction of the initial residual, and once a full step is taken all later iterates are primal feasible.

assertions.value: The book gives Algorithm 10.2, the infeasible start Newton method: compute primal and dual Newton steps, backtrack on the norm of the residual with the condition that the residual norm must fall below one minus alpha t times the old norm, update both x and nu, and stop when A x equals b and the residual norm is at most epsilon.

assertions.value: The book states that the residual-based line search must terminate in a finite number of steps because the derivative result shows the exit condition holds for small t, and that once a feasible iterate is obtained the infeasible start search direction coincides with the feasible Newton direction.

assertions.value: The book states that the main advantage of the infeasible start Newton method is simpler initialization: when the domain is simple and known to contain a point satisfying A x equals b (for example the positive orthant in analytic centering), any point in the domain such as the all-ones vector can start the method, avoiding a phase I method; when the domain is all of R n there is no advantage other than convenience.
quotes: The main advantage of the infeasible start Newton method is in the initialization required.
using the infeasible start Newton method, with any positive initial point, e.g., x(0) = 1.

assertions.value: The book states the disadvantage of using the infeasible start Newton method when a strictly feasible start is unknown: there is no clear way to detect that no strictly feasible point exists, since the residual norm simply converges slowly to a positive value, whereas phase I methods determine this unambiguously, and convergence before feasibility can be slow.
quotes: there is no clear way to detect that there exists no strictly feasible point; the norm of the residual will simply converge, slowly, to some positive value.

assertions.value: The book defines a solution of a two-player zero-sum game as a saddle point, a pair with the payoff at the saddle point no more than the payoff at the first player's best change and no less than at the second's; when it exists, there is no advantage to moving second, and for a differentiable convex-concave payoff a saddle point is characterized by zero gradient.

assertions.value: The book states the inequality constrained problem form for interior-point methods: minimize a convex twice continuously differentiable objective subject to convex twice continuously differentiable inequality constraints and A x equals b with rank A equal to p smaller than n, assuming it is solvable and strictly feasible, so Slater's condition holds and dual optimal points exist which with x-star satisfy the KKT conditions.

This means that Slater's constraint qualification holds, so there exist dual optimal λ⋆ ∈ Rm, ν⋆ ∈ Rp
assertions.certainty_reason: The book states its own scope at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that interior-point methods solve the problem by applying Newton's method to a sequence of equality constrained problems or modified KKT conditions, that the book concentrates on the barrier method with a proof of convergence and a complexity analysis, and that it describes a simple primal-dual interior-point method without an analysis.
quotes: We will concentrate on a particular interior-point algorithm, the barrier method, for which we give a proof of convergence and a complexity analysis.
but do not give an analysis.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book states its own scope at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book describes a hierarchy of algorithms in which equality constrained quadratic problems are solved analytically, Newton's method reduces a twice differentiable equality constrained problem to a sequence of such quadratic problems, and interior-point methods reduce problems with inequality constraints to a sequence of equality constrained problems.
quotes: Interior-point methods form the next level in the hierarchy: They solve an optimization problem with linear equality and inequality constraints by reducing it to a sequence of linear equality constrained problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that LPs, QPs, QCQPs and geometric programs in convex form are directly in the required form, that nondifferentiable problems such as piecewise-linear minimization can be reformulated into it, and that SOCPs and SDPs are not readily recast but are handled by extensions of interior-point methods to generalized inequalities.
quotes: Other convex optimization problems, such as SOCPs and SDPs, are not readily recast in the required form, but can be handled by extensions of interior-point methods to problems with generalized inequalities
assertions.certainty_reason: The book states its own scope at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book defines the logarithmic barrier approximation of the indicator function of the nonpositive reals as minus one over t times the log of minus u, with parameter t controlling accuracy; it is convex, nondecreasing, differentiable and closed, and the approximation becomes more accurate as t increases.
quotes: As t increases, the approximation becomes more accurate.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book defines the logarithmic barrier of the problem as minus the sum of the logs of minus each inequality constraint function, with domain the strictly feasible points of the inequalities, and notes it grows without bound as any constraint function approaches zero, whatever the positive parameter t.
quotes: is called the logarithmic barrier or log barrier for the problem (11.1).
No matter what value the positive parameter t has, the logarithmic barrier grows without bound if fi(x) → 0, for any i.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that the approximation improves as t grows, but for large t the barrier objective is difficult to minimize by Newton's method because its Hessian varies rapidly near the boundary of the feasible set, which is circumvented by solving a sequence of problems with increasing t, each started at the solution for the previous t.
quotes: the function f0 + (1/t)φ is difficult to minimize by Newton's method, since its Hessian varies rapidly near the boundary of the feasible set.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book defines the central path as the set of solutions x-star of t, for t greater than zero, of minimizing t times the objective plus the barrier subject to A x equals b, assuming a unique solution exists for each t; central points are characterized as strictly feasible with a dual vector nu-hat such that t times the gradient of the objective plus the gradient of the barrier plus A transpose nu-hat is zero.
quotes: The central path associated with problem (11.1) is defined as the set of points x⋆(t), t > 0, which we call the central points.
Points on the central path are characterized by the following necessary and sufficient conditions
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book gives, for the inequality form LP, the barrier gradient as A transpose d and Hessian as A transpose diag(d) squared times A with d i equal to one over (b i minus a i transpose x), and states the Hessian is nonsingular if and only if A has rank n; the centrality condition is t c plus A transpose d equal to zero, which says the hyperplane c transpose x equals its central-point value is tangent to the barrier's level set.
quotes: Since x is strictly feasible, we have d ≻ 0, so the Hessian of φ is nonsingular if and only if A has rank n.
the hyperplane cT x = cT x⋆(t) is tangent to the level set of φ through x⋆(t).

assertions.value: The book proves that every central point yields a dual feasible pair, lambda-star of t equal to minus one over t times f i at x-star of t and nu-star of t equal to nu-hat over t, because x-star of t minimizes the Lagrangian at that pair, giving a finite dual function equal to the objective at x-star of t minus m over t.
assertions.anchor: Section 11.2.2, Dual points from central path, PDF p.579-580
quotes: Every central point yields a dual feasible point, and hence a lower bound on the optimal value p⋆.

assertions.value: The book states that the central path converges to the optimal point as t goes to infinity, and that this confirms the intuition that x-star of t converges to an optimal point, since it is no more than m over t suboptimal.

assertions.value: The book gives a mechanics interpretation of the central path: constraint forces repel a particle from the boundary of the feasible set with potential equal to the barrier, an objective force minus t times the gradient pulls it toward smaller objective, and the central point is where they balance; for an LP the constraint force is inversely proportional to the distance to the constraint hyperplane.
assertions.anchor: Section 11.2.2, Force field interpretation, PDF p.581-582
quotes: The central point x⋆(t) is the point where the constraint forces exactly balance the objective force felt by the particle.
each constraint hyperplane has an associated repulsive force, given by the inverse distance to the hyperplane.
