assertions.value: The book states that taking t equal to m over epsilon and solving the single centering problem guarantees an epsilon-suboptimal solution, but that this method, which can work for small problems, good starting points and moderate accuracy, does not work well otherwise and is rarely, if ever, used.
quotes: it does not work well in other cases. As a result it is rarely, if ever, used.

assertions.value: The book states the barrier method, also called the path-following method and originally the sequential unconstrained minimization technique of Fiacco and McCormick in the 1960s: from a strictly feasible point and a starting parameter t, repeatedly compute the central point by Newton's method starting from the previous one, stop when m over t is below epsilon, otherwise multiply t by a factor mu greater than one.
quotes: When the method was first proposed by Fiacco and McCormick in the 1960s, it was called the sequential unconstrained minimization technique (SUMT).
Today the method is usually called the barrier method or path-following method.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book defines each execution of the centering step as an outer iteration and each Newton step within it as an inner iteration, and states that at each inner step there is a primal feasible point while a dual feasible point exists only at the end of each outer step.
quotes: At each inner step, we have a primal feasible point; we have a dual feasible point, however, only at the end of each outer (centering) step.
assertions.certainty_reason: The book defines it at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that exact centering is not necessary, since inexact centering still yields points converging to an optimum, though the derived dual points are then not exactly dual feasible unless a correction term is added; it adds that the cost of an extremely accurate minimizer is only marginally more than a good one, a few Newton steps at most.
assertions.anchor: Section 11.3.1, Accuracy of centering, PDF p.584
quotes: inexact centering will still yield a sequence of points x(k) that converges to an optimal point.
is only marginally more, i.e., a few Newton steps at most.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states the trade-off in the barrier parameter factor mu: a value near one needs few Newton steps per outer iteration but many outer iterations, and a large value needs fewer outer iterations but many more inner iterations; in practice for mu from around 3 to 100 the total number of Newton steps stays approximately constant, values around 10 to 20 work well, and the best worst-case bound is obtained with mu near one.
assertions.anchor: Section 11.3.1, Choice of mu, PDF p.584
quotes: For μ in a fairly large range, from around 3 to 100 or so, the two effects nearly cancel, so the total number of Newton steps remains approximately constant.
values from around 10 to 20 or so seem to work well.
When the parameter μ is chosen to give the best worst-case bound on the total number of Newton steps required, values of μ near one are used.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that too large an initial t makes the first outer iteration need too many iterations and too small makes extra outer iterations necessary; a reasonable choice makes m over t-zero of the same order as the initial suboptimality, or mu times it, and with a known dual feasible point of gap eta one can take t-zero equal to m over eta.
assertions.anchor: Section 11.3.1, Choice of t-zero, PDF p.585
quotes: For example, if a dual feasible point λ, ν is known, with duality gap η = f0(x(0)) − g(λ, ν), then we can take t(0) = m/η.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The book states that in a variation of the barrier method the infeasible start Newton method is used for the centering steps, so the initial point need only satisfy the inequality constraints strictly and not A x equal to b; for a strictly feasible problem a full Newton step is taken at some point in the first centering step, after which iterates are primal feasible and the algorithm coincides with the standard barrier method.
assertions.anchor: Section 11.3.1, Infeasible start Newton method, PDF p.585
quotes: a full Newton step is taken at some point during the first centering step, and thereafter, the iterates are all primal feasible, and the algorithm coincides with the (standard) barrier method.

assertions.value: The authors state that the slow growth of the number of Newton steps with problem dimension is typical for the barrier method in general: it grows very slowly, is almost always around a few tens, while the effort per Newton step does grow with the dimensions.

assertions.value: The book states that for the standard Newton method it suffices that the function t f0 plus the barrier has a closed initial sublevel set, bounded inverse KKT matrix and Lipschitz Hessian for t at least the initial t, that the infeasible start conditions suffice if that method is used, and that adding a norm bound constraint on x makes the function strongly convex for all t, guaranteeing convergence of the centering steps (given closed functions).

it follows that tf0 + φ is strongly convex, for every t ≥ 0; in particular convergence of Newton's method, for the centering steps, is guaranteed.

quotes: We will see (in §11.5) that this issue can be resolved, for problems that satisfy certain self-concordance conditions.
Numerical evidence suggests that for a wide variety of problems, this is not the case; the centering problems appear to require a nearly constant number of Newton steps to solve, even as t increases.

assertions.value: The book states that the barrier method requires a strictly feasible start, and when none is known a phase I stage computes one or finds the constraints infeasible; the basic phase I problem minimizes a bound s on the maximum infeasibility subject to f i of x at most s and A x equal to b, which is always strictly feasible.
quotes: The barrier method requires a strictly feasible starting point x(0).
This problem is always strictly feasible, since we can choose x(0) as starting point for x

assertions.value: The book states that in the basic phase I method one need not solve to high accuracy: for a negative optimal value one can stop as soon as s is negative, and for a positive optimal value one can stop when a dual feasible point with positive dual objective is found, from which a certificate of infeasibility is constructed; a zero optimal value attained at s equal to zero means feasible but not strictly feasible, and a zero value not attained means infeasible.
quotes: we can terminate when s < 0.

assertions.value: The book states that in practice one cannot determine exactly that the phase I optimal value is zero, and an algorithm instead concludes that its absolute value is below a small epsilon, which establishes that the inequalities with right side minus epsilon are infeasible while those with epsilon are feasible.
quotes: This allows us to conclude that the inequalities fi(x) ≤ −ǫ are infeasible, while the inequalities fi(x) ≤ ǫ are feasible.

assertions.value: The book states that the complexity analysis of the barrier method via self-concordance applies to many common problems and gives a rigorous bound on the total number of Newton steps and a justification for the observation that centering problems do not become more difficult as t increases.

assertions.value: The book states that for a closed strictly convex self-concordant function the number of Newton iterations is bounded above by the initial suboptimality over gamma plus c, where gamma depends only on the backtracking parameters through twenty minus eight alpha over alpha beta times (one minus two alpha) squared, and c depends only on the tolerance and can reasonably be approximated by six; the bound is quite conservative.

assertions.value: The book gives an upper bound on the total number of Newton steps of the barrier method, not counting the initial centering step, equal to the number of outer steps log(m over t-zero epsilon) over log mu times the per-outer bound; for fixed mu and m it is proportional to the log of the required duality gap reduction, so the method converges at least linearly, and for fixed mu and reduction it grows linearly with m and is independent of n and p.
quotes: We can therefore say that the barrier method converges at least linearly, since the number of steps required to reach a given precision grows logarithmically with the inverse of the precision.

assertions.value: The appendix states that in the factor-solve method the total flop count is f plus s, with f the factorization cost and s the solve cost, that the factorization often dominates, and that for m right-hand sides with the same matrix the cost is f plus m s because factorization is done once, so a small number of systems can be solved at essentially the cost of one.
quotes: The total flop count for solving Ax = b using this factor-solve method is f +s, where f is the flop count for computing the factorization, and s is the total flop count for the solve step.
Since we only factor A once, the total effort is f + ms.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that the inverse can be computed by one factorization and n solves, so the cost is f plus n s.
quotes: This requires one factorization and n solves, so the cost is f + ns.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that every nonsingular matrix can be factored as A equal to P L U with P a permutation, L unit lower triangular and U upper triangular, computed by Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting at a cost of two thirds n cubed flops, and that solving by LU costs two thirds n cubed plus two n squared flops, with the permutation step free.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C.3.1, Algorithm C.1, PDF p.682
quotes: The cost is (2/3)n3 flops if no structure in A is exploited, which is the case we consider first.
The total cost is (2/3)n3 + 2n2, or (2/3)n3 flops if we keep only the leading term.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that computing the inverse by solving for each unit vector using the LU factorization costs eight thirds n cubed, about three n cubed flops, and that for m right-hand sides the cost is two thirds n cubed plus two m n squared.
quotes: This costs (8/3)n3, i.e., about 3n3 flops.
the cost is (2/3)n3 + 2mn2, since we factor A once
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that for a banded matrix of bandwidth k much smaller than n, an LU factorization can be computed in roughly 4 n k squared flops, the upper factor has bandwidth at most 2k, the substitutions cost order 6 n k, and so the linear equations can be solved in about 4 n k squared flops.
quotes: In this case an LU factorization of A can be computed in roughly 4nk2 flops.
so the forward and back substitutions can be carried out in order 6nk flops.
Therefore if A is banded, the linear equations Ax = b can be solved in about 4nk2 flops.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that for a sparse matrix the LU factorization usually includes row and column permutations chosen in part to yield sparse factors, that its cost depends in a complicated way on size, nonzeros, sparsity pattern and algorithm but is often dramatically smaller than a dense factorization, and in many cases grows approximately linearly with n for large n.
quotes: In many cases the cost grows approximately linearly with n, when n is large.

assertions.value: The appendix states that a symmetric positive definite matrix can be factored as L L transpose with L lower triangular with positive diagonal (the Cholesky factorization), uniquely determined, at a dense cost of one third n cubed flops, half the cost of an LU factorization, so solving by Cholesky costs one third n cubed plus two n squared, roughly one third n cubed flops.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C.3.2, Algorithm C.2, PDF p.683-684
quotes: The cost of computing the Cholesky factorization of a dense matrix, i.e., without exploiting any structure, is (1/3)n3 flops, half the cost of an LU factorization.
The total cost is (1/3)n3 + 2n2, or roughly (1/3)n3 flops.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that for a symmetric positive definite matrix banded with bandwidth k the Cholesky factor is banded with bandwidth k, computed in n k squared flops, with a solve step cost of 4 n k flops.
quotes: its Cholesky factor L is banded with bandwidth k, and can be calculated in nk2 flops.
The cost of the associated solve step is 4nk flops.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that a sparse symmetric positive definite matrix is factored as P L L transpose P transpose with a permutation chosen by heuristics, that any permutation gives a valid unique Cholesky factor but can greatly affect the sparsity of the factor, and illustrates with an arrow pattern that a very sparse matrix can have an almost completely dense Cholesky factor, while moving the dense row and column to the end gives a very sparse factor.
assertions.anchor: Example C.1, Appendix C.3.2, PDF p.684
quotes: The choice of P , however, can greatly affect the sparsity of the factor L, which in turn can greatly affect the efficiency of solving Ax = b.
Although the matrix A is very sparse (most of its rows have just two nonzero elements), its Cholesky factors are almost completely dense.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that for sparse Cholesky the permutation and sparsity pattern of L can be determined from the sparsity pattern alone, a step called symbolic factorization whose cost is significant and often comparable to the numerical factorization, so that m systems with the same sparsity pattern cost f-symbolic plus m times (f-numeric plus s), against m times (f-symbolic plus f-numeric plus s) if repeated; in contrast, sparse LU permutations depend on numerical values.
quotes: This is useful in many applications, because the cost of the symbolic factorization is significant, and often comparable to the numerical factorization.
In contrast, the permutation matrices in a sparse LU factorization do depend on the numerical values in A
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that every nonsingular symmetric matrix can be factored as P L D L transpose P transpose with D block diagonal with 1 by 1 and 2 by 2 blocks, computed in a third of n cubed flops without exploiting structure, with Cholesky as a special case, and that in a sparse LDL transpose factorization the permutation also depends on the nonzero values, unlike sparse Cholesky.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C.3.3, Algorithm C.3, PDF p.686
quotes: with nonsingular 1 × 1 and 2 × 2 diagonal blocks.
An LDLT factorization can be computed in (1/3)n3 flops, if no structure of A is exploited.
it also depends on the particular nonzero values in the matrix A.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that solving A x equal to b by eliminating a block of variables reduces to the Schur complement system, whose matrix S equals A22 minus A21 A11 inverse A12 is nonsingular if and only if A is nonsingular, that block elimination is equivalent to a block LU factorization, and that for a dense unstructured matrix it gives no advantage.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C.4.1, Algorithm C.4, PDF p.686-687
quotes: For a dense unstructured matrix, this approach gives no advantage.
The Schur complement S is nonsingular if and only if A is nonsingular.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix derives that block elimination costs f plus n2 s plus 2 n2 squared n1 plus two thirds n2 cubed flops, which for an unstructured block equals two thirds (n1 plus n2) cubed, the same as a standard LU factorization, so there is no advantage unless the structure of the eliminated block allows efficient factoring and solving.
quotes: In other words, solving a set of equations by block elimination gives no advantage when no structure of A11 is exploited.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that eliminating a diagonal block leaves a cost of 2 n2 squared n1 plus two thirds n2 cubed, growing only linearly in n1 rather than cubically, that eliminating a banded block gives the same leading cost (the arrow matrix case), and that eliminating a block diagonal block with small blocks gives dramatic savings, the partially separable case with a complicating variable.
quotes: yields 2n22n1 + (2/3)n23, flops, which is far smaller
In particular, the flop count of the standard method grows cubicly in n1, whereas for block elimination the flop count grows only linearly in n1.
Block elimination can solve linear equations with arrow structure far more efficiently than the standard method.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that when the eliminated block is sparse and the other blocks dense with n2 much smaller than n1, the matrix is sparse with a few dense rows and columns, that a sparse solver applied to the whole matrix is more straightforward than block elimination but often slower when structure in the other blocks can be exploited, and that exploiting symmetry saves around a factor of two.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C.4.1 and C.4.2, PDF p.690
quotes: This is more straightforward than using block elimination, but often slower, especially in applications where we can exploit structure in the other blocks
Overall the savings over the nonsymmetric case is around a factor of two.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that block elimination reduces to block forward substitution when the upper right block is zero, that when A11 is block diagonal with maximum block size l and the other blocks are banded with bandwidth k the Schur complement is banded with bandwidth 2k plus l so Ax equal to b can be solved with a flop count growing linearly with n, and that for KKT structure the Schur complement is negative definite so Cholesky applies.
assertions.anchor: Examples C.2 to C.4, Appendix C.4.2, PDF p.691
quotes: A21A−111A12 is banded with bandwidth 2k + l.
we can solve Ax = b with a number of flops that grows linearly with n.
The Schur complement S = −A1T2A−111A12 is negative definite, so we can factor −S using a Cholesky factorization.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix derives the matrix inversion lemma (Sherman-Woodbury-Morrison formula): the inverse of A plus B C equals A inverse minus A inverse B times the inverse of (I plus C A inverse B) times C A inverse, by introducing a new variable y equal to C x, so that A plus B C is the Schur complement of minus the identity in a larger system, and eliminating x from it.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C.4.3, equations (C.7) to (C.9), PDF p.692
quotes: This is known as the matrix inversion lemma, or the Sherman-Woodbury-Morrison formula.
Note that our original coefficient matrix, A + BC, is the Schur complement of −I in the larger matrix that appears in (C.8).
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that for diagonal A and a rank p product B C, forming A plus B C and factoring it costs 2 p n squared plus two thirds n cubed flops, while evaluating the matrix inversion lemma right to left costs 2 p squared n plus two thirds p cubed, more efficient when p is less than n and linear in n for fixed small p.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C.4.3, Diagonal or sparse plus low rank, PDF p.693
quotes: The total cost is 2p2n + (2/3)p3 flops, dropping dominated terms.
so the total cost is 2pn2 + (2/3)n3 flops.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that for a sparse nonsingular A and dense B and C, solving via the matrix inversion lemma with a sparse LU factorization of A costs f plus p s plus 2 p squared n plus two thirds p cubed flops, much lower than forming A plus B C and using a dense LU when f is much smaller than two thirds n cubed and s much smaller than 2 n squared.
quotes: This gives us a total cost of f + ps + 2p2n + (2/3)p3 flops.
If f ≪ (2/3)n3 and s ≪ 2n2, this is much lower than the complexity of the first method.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that solving the larger augmented system directly with a sparse LU solver can be much faster than a dense solver when A is very sparse and p is small, is closely related to the matrix inversion lemma method, gives no control over the permutations chosen, and is nonetheless attractive because it is easier to implement and numerically more stable.
assertions.anchor: Remark C.3, Appendix C.4.3, PDF p.694
quotes: It is easier to implement than the method based on the matrix inversion lemma, and it is numerically more stable.

assertions.value: The appendix states that, using the matrix inversion lemma, the solution of a rank-one updated system can be computed from the solution of the original system by factoring A once, so that both systems cost f plus 2 s in total, against 2 times (f plus s) if the second is solved from scratch.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C.4.3, Low rank updates, PDF p.694
quotes: The overall cost is f + 2s, as opposed to 2(f + s) if we were to solve for x ̃ from scratch.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that for an underdetermined system with full row rank p less than n, a particular solution can be found by inverting a p by p nonsingular submatrix of A and setting the other variables to zero at the cost of factoring plus one solve, and the full solution set parametrized with the nullspace basis F, at cost f plus s times (n minus p plus one).
quotes: Then the cost of finding one solution of (C.11) is f + s.
The cost of parametrizing all solutions (i.e., calculating F and xˆ) is f + s(n − p + 1).
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that a full column rank matrix can be factored as Q1 Q2 times R and zero, with R upper triangular, in 2 p squared (n minus p over three) flops, that applying it to the transpose of A gives a particular solution Q1 R inverse transpose b and a nullspace basis Q2, and that it is the most common method for underdetermined equations with the drawback that it is difficult to exploit sparsity since Q is usually dense.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C.5, The QR factorization, PDF p.696
quotes: The QR factorization can be calculated in 2p2(n − p/3) flops.
One drawback is that it is difficult to exploit sparsity.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix states that a full column rank rectangular matrix can be factored as P L U at a cost of two thirds p cubed plus p squared times (n minus p) flops without structure, that a sparse rectangular LU can be calculated very efficiently, and that the LU of the transpose of A parametrizes the solution set of an underdetermined system.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C.5, LU factorization of a rectangular matrix, PDF p.697
quotes: The cost is (2/3)p3 + p2(n − p) flops if no structure in C is exploited.
The LU factorization of a sparse rectangular matrix can be calculated very efficiently
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated and proved or derived in the text at the anchor.

assertions.value: The appendix bibliography states that LAPACK provides high-quality implementations of common dense linear algebra algorithms and is built on the BLAS, a library of basic vector and matrix routines that can be customized to specific computer architectures, and lists sparse solver codes including SPOOLES, SuperLU, UMFPACK and WSMP.
quotes: LAPACK is built upon the Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS), a library of routines for basic vector and matrix operations
including SPOOLES [APWW99], SuperLU [DGL03], UMFPACK [Dav03], and WSMP [Gup00]

quotes: f is a function on the set dom f ⊆ A into the set B.
Derivative (Jacobian) matrix of function f .

quotes: Generalized inequality induced by proper cone K.
Matrix inequality between symmetric matrices X and Y .

quotes: Symmetric positive semidefinite, positive definite, n × n matrices.
Moore-Penrose or pseudo-inverse of matrix X.

papers.title_in_file: High-Performance Computing with Quantum Processing Units
papers.what_it_is: A conceptual analysis of how QPUs can be integrated into HPC systems through loose (client-server) and tight (accelerator) integration paths, with proposed QPU performance metrics.

existing.note: Value is right. The stored anchor says 6 Conclusions, but the paper's Conclusions is Section 5, p.11. The paper also says a quantum interconnect is clearly able to enhance functionality, which the value states in part.
existing.value: The authors state that a quantum interconnect can enlarge the set of accessible register states but that it is unclear whether it would give a net benefit, because entanglement between nodes exposes the system to a more serious fault model with correlated errors.
quotes: It is clear that a quantum interconnect can enhance system functionality by enlarging the set of accessible register states, but it remains unclear if the interconnect would provide a net beneﬁt.
the entanglement established between nodes by the interconnect would expose the system to a potentially more serious fault model, in which correlated errors lead to a cascade of failures across QPUs
existing.certainty_reason: An author claim, not tested in the paper.

existing.note: Value is right. The stored anchor says 6 Conclusions, but the paper's Conclusions is Section 5, p.11.
existing.value: The authors state that existing metrics for conventional computing do not capture all aspects of QPU behavior and suggest new features to track.
quotes: Existing metrics for conventional computing do not capture all aspects of the QPU behavior, and we have suggested several new features that need to be tracked when tuning system performance
existing.certainty_reason: An author claim, not tested in the paper.

existing.note: Value is right and complete. The stored anchor (Abstract) is right. Small point: the Introduction says Section 3 examines three multi-processing models, and Section 3 shows several architectures (Figures 2 to 5) under the two paths. The tight path is also stated in Section 3 as assuming the QPU hardware requirements can be eased.
existing.value: The authors identify two pathways for integrating QPUs into HPC systems, tight integration that assumes infrastructure bottlenecks can be overcome and loose integration that assumes they cannot.
quotes: We identify two integration pathways that are differentiated by infrastructure constraints on the QPU and the use cases expected for the HPC system.
This includes a tight integration that assumes infrastructure bottlenecks can be overcome as well as a loose integration that assumes they cannot.
existing.certainty_reason: The abstract states the scope and the two pathways of the paper's analysis.
existing.reader_inference: The paper is a conceptual architecture analysis. No experiment supports either pathway.

assertions.value: The authors state that they analyze the integration of QPUs into modern HPC architectures, with an emphasis on conceptual differences between the conventional and quantum computing models that may challenge integration.
quotes: We analyze the integration of these quantum processing units (QPUs) for modern HPC architectures.
We place an emphasis on conceptual differences between the conventional and quantum computing models that may be expected to challenge integration.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the scope of their own analysis in Section 1.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no experiment or measurement; it is a conceptual architecture analysis.

assertions.value: The authors define a QPU as a computational unit that uses quantum computing principles to perform a task.
quotes: We deﬁne a QPU to be a computational unit that uses quantum computing principles to perform a task.
assertions.certainty_reason: A definition the paper states in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors define a QPU to include a QRAM that applies low-level gates to register elements, a quantum control unit (QCU) that parses programs into instructions, and a classical controller interface that defines how the host CPU interacts with the QPU.
quotes: We deﬁne a QPU to include a QRAM that applies low-level gates to register elements, a quantum control unit (QCU) that parses programs into instructions, and a classical controller interface that deﬁnes how the central processing unit (CPU) within a host system interacts with the QPU.
assertions.certainty_reason: A definition the paper states in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the unique ISA of each technology base shows a need for abstraction of the QCU interface, and that standardizing the QCU interface will promote robust QPU design across technologies and assist integration into larger systems.
quotes: The unique ISA deﬁning each technology base indicates the need for abstraction of the QCU interface.
The standardization of the QCU interface will not only promote robust QPU design across different technologies but also assist integration of these devices into larger system designs.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that interfaces which mask quantum hardware details from the software developer are especially important for maintaining existing applications across HPC environments, and that an API requiring developers to put quantum instructions directly into the code base will prevent adoption because of the burden of code rewriting.
quotes: Interfaces that encapsulate and mask quantum hardware details from the software developer are especially important for maintaining existing applications across a variety of HPC environments.

an application program interface that requires software developers to integrate quantum processing instructions directly into the code base will prevent its adoption (due to the burden of code rewriting)
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the interface between classical and quantum computational models, exposed by domain decomposition, is not yet well defined, that translation between the models may be theoretically possible, and that making these interfaces efficient and robust is an outstanding concern. They also state that development of the CPU-QPU interfaces is still an open question.
quotes: domain decomposition exposes an interface between classical and quantum computational models that is not yet well deﬁned
Translation between computational models may be theoretically possible but making these interfaces efﬁcient and robust is an outstanding concern.
Development of these interfaces is still an open question
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that many quantum algorithms lack clearly defined kernels that can be off-loaded to a quantum accelerator, that the mixture of computational models stymies use of conventional SIMD and MIMD parallelism, and that quantum algorithms frequently intentionally avoid domain decomposition.
quotes: many quantum algorithms lack clearly deﬁned kernels that can be off-loaded to a quantum computational accelerator
The mixture of computational models also stymies efforts to leverage conventional notions of SIMD and multiple-instruction multiple-data (MIMD) parallelism.
quantum algorithms frequently intentionally avoid this type of problem partitioning
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that all quantum computational models offer identical computational power from a complexity perspective, but differ in hardware implementations and principles of operation.
quotes: While all the models offer identical computational power from a complexity perspective, they do differ with respect to hardware implementations and principles of operation.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no citation or proof for this statement at this point.

assertions.value: The authors state that intermediate computations cannot be copied during communication between QPUs, as a consequence of the no-cloning theorem, so communication must use either direct transmission or teleportation.
quotes: However, a notable feature of quantum computing is that intermediate computations cannot be copied during the communication.
Instead, communication between QPUs must use either direct transmission or teleportation [Nielsen and Chuang 2000].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that teleportation transfers a register value using pre-existing entanglement between QPUs, and that it also needs classical side-channel information that is generally much less than the information needed to describe the value of the quantum register.
quotes: teleportation uses pre-existing entanglement between the QPUs to perform the data transfer
this classical information is generally much less than the information needed to describe the value of the quantum register
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that many technologies for a fully functional QPU currently require bulky and costly infrastructure, including dilution refrigerators, electromagnetic shielding and ultra-high vacuum enclosures, and that this is a significant obstacle to integration.
quotes: A signiﬁcant obstacle to integration is the physical hardware requirements of current experimental quantum computing devices.
Many technologies that could be used to realize a fully functional QPU currently require bulky and costly infrastructure.
This includes the use of dilution refrigerators to suppress thermal noise, electromagnetic shielding to avert ambient energy, and ultra-high vacuum enclosures to prevent device contamination.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that they anticipate QPU requirements will ease with future device development, citing work on ultra-cold operation of FPGAs to drive silicon qubits as suggesting a path to integrating the QPU control interface within the dilution refrigerator, and work on miniaturized control electronics for linear optical quantum chips.
quotes: We anticipate that QPU requirements will ease with future device development and reﬁned engineering principles.

recent work on ultra-cold operation of ﬁeld-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) to drive silicon qubits suggests there is a path toward integration of the QPU control interface within the dilution refrigerator
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors define loose integration as QPUs remaining isolated operational elements that interact with a host HPC system through a network interface, which is effectively a client-server model in which the QC server may be on a dedicated network or part of a larger computational grid.
quotes: In the loose integration path, QPUs remain as isolated operational elements that must interact with a host HPC system using a network interface.
This is effectively a client-server model as shown in Figure 3 where the quantum computing (QC) server may either be on a dedicated network or part of a larger computational grid.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its loose integration path in Section 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the client-server model the entry point into the system remains the primary bottleneck, and that access to each QPU must still be provisioned by the QC control system.
quotes: However, the entry point into the system remains the primary bottleneck.
access to each QPU must still be provisioned by the QC control system
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the client-server model forces a tradeoff between communication latency and the speedup gained from using a QPU instead of a CPU, that the tradeoff is advantageous when communication time is offset by the QPU speedup, and that it depends on problem type and size.
quotes: The demands of the client-server model in Figure 3 force a tradeoff between the communication latency and the computational speedup gained from using a QPU instead of a CPU (or some other local resource).
This tradeoff is advantageous when the communication time is offset by the QPU speedup, but this will depend on problem type as well as size.
Latencies will contribute to overall execution timing and, depending on problem and program structure, could partially negate quantum computational advantages.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the client-server model is likely to be broadly useful only when the computational gain over conventional approaches is significant, which adds emphasis to the importance of the underlying quantum algorithm.
quotes: Therefore, the client-server model is likely to be broadly useful
only when the computational gain over conventional approaches is signiﬁcant. This adds emphasis to the importance of the underlying quantum algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a server with q QPUs, each with an n-qubit register, the server Hilbert space dimension is q times two to the power n when the QPUs are isolated (printed flat as q2n), and two to the power n times q (printed flat as 2nq) when a quantum interconnect links them, and that this exponential increase in capacity is not a guarantee of computational speedup.
quotes: For a system containing q QPUs, the server can support classical MIMD parallelism with each node performing an isolated job.
the dimension of the server Hilbert space is q2n given an n-qubit register on each node
the presence of a quantum interconnect linking the individual QPUs offers a Hilbert space of 2nq
This exponential increase in server capacity with node number is not a guarantee of computational speedup.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer printed the exponents flat; the intended forms are probably q times two to the n and two to the n times q.

assertions.value: The authors state that the cloud-based quantum computing model may be especially attractive for blind quantum computing, which lets a user submit a job request without revealing details of the data or instructions.
quotes: The cloud-based quantum computing model may be especially attractive for blind quantum computing, which permits a user to submit a job request without revealing details about either the data or instructions [Broadbent et al. 2009].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without evidence or test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the goal of the tight integration design is to move the QPU closer to the host node to eliminate communication latency and maximize computational speedup, and that the design assumes QPU hardware requirements can be eased enough for a tightly connected single-system model.
quotes: The goal of this design is to move the QPU closer to the host node in order to eliminate communication latency and maximize computational speedup.
This design assumes the hardware requirements for QPUs can
be eased to the point that a single, tightly connected single-system model can be created.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the goal and assumption of its tight integration path in Section 3.

assertions.value: The authors describe a shared resource model in which multiple CPU nodes interact with a single QPU node, state that it still represents a bottleneck but that tighter integration alleviates some of the overhead of the loose model, and that data from multiple CPUs can be aggregated by the QPU.
quotes: Figure 4 (left) represents a ﬁrst design based on a shared resource model that permits multiple CPU nodes to interact with a single QPU node.
This communication design also represents a bottleneck but the tighter integration alleviates some of the overhead required in the loose model.
data from multiple CPUs can be aggregated by the QPU

Metric Number of Qubits FTQEC Qubit Overhead FTQEC Gate Overhead Clock Cycles Per Gate FTQEC Latency Number of Gates Sample Rate

the longest duration gate within a QRAM can serve as a worst-case measure of performance, while the shortest gate reﬂects best time cost
The timing difference between these instructions offers a measure of the spread in QRAM performance on

The use of statistical sampling to derive the ﬁnal result requires conﬁdence levels that determine the number of required samples and therefore total duration of the program.

in a high-performance setting, the rate of entangling and preserving entanglement between nodes represents a potential bottleneck for the system

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Radio Astronomy: Data Encodings and Quantum Image Processing
papers.version_note: The text is arXiv:2310.12084v3 (9 Feb 2024); the record id says 2024 and the file name says 2023 (v1 date).
papers.what_it_is: A theory and simulation study of quantum image encodings (binary, Quantum Lattice, FRQI, QPIE), the QFT and a variational gain-calibration algorithm for radio interferometry, run on a noiseless simulator with a gate-error estimate.

existing.note: The abstract sentence is quoted correctly, but Section 5 limits it: the exponential speedup is stated for identifying one bright source (a number of shots of order N), relative to the FFT, and under the optimal QPIE circuit depth. For a number of sources proportional to N squared the paper finds advantage over the DFT but not over the FFT. Section 7 then shows the optimal-depth circuit is impractical on current hardware, and Section 4 states that no gate or measurement errors were modeled.
existing.value: The authors state that the exponential speedup is for identifying one bright source in an image, which needs Nshots = O(N) shots, and is stated relative to the FFT, under the optimal QPIE circuit depth; for identifying a number of sources proportional to N squared, the shots needed give quantum advantage over the DFT but not the FFT.
quotes: For identifying and locating bright radio sources, quantum computing can offer an exponential speedup over classical algorithms, even when accounting for data encoding cost and repeated circuit evaluations.
In the case of identifying one bright source in an image, Nshots = O(N) shots are needed, offering exponential speedup over the FFT.
In the case of identifying ∝ N2 sources in an image, Nshots = O(N2) shots are needed, which has quantum advantage over the DFT but not the FFT.
If we consider the optimal QPIE circuit depth of O( f (N2)) = O(log2N × log2N), and the optimal number of shots needed to reconstruct sources Nshots the true complexity of the QFT is:
existing.reader_inference: The speedup is an asymptotic scaling argument (Equation 8 and Table 1), not a measured wall-clock result; the abstract's wording does not carry the single-source and optimal-depth conditions.

existing.value: The authors state that measurement of the quantum state is a probabilistic result which destroys the superposition, so multiple measurements require re-encoding and re-measuring the state, which can undermine quantum advantage.
quotes: measurement of the quantum state is a probabilistic result which destroys the superposition. To perform multiple measurements, one must re-encode and re-measure the state, which can undermine quantum advantage.
To generate multiple measurements of a quantum image, the entire image representation must be re-encoded and re-measured.
existing.reader_inference: The paper adds that quantum random access memory or future quantum memory might remove the re-encoding requirement; it does not test this.

existing.note: The first quote is in the Conclusion only (the Abstract holds the toy-pipeline sentence, not the QPIE sentence). The paper limits the claim: the fidelity statement is for source identification where lower image accuracy is tolerable; a high-fidelity image needs an intractably large number of shots, and the authors say QPIE may not suit high-fidelity analysis. Experiments ran on a noiseless simulator.
existing.value: The authors report that, in a toy image reconstruction pipeline, of the different quantum image encodings the QPIE encoding offers excellent algorithmic speedup without sacrificing image fidelity, in cases where lower image accuracy is tolerable; they state that QPIE encodings may not be suitable for high-fidelity image analysis demanded by extended source structure or cosmological studies, and that if a high-fidelity image is needed the number of shots becomes intractably large.
existing.anchor: Abstract p.1; Section 5 p.6; Conclusion p.9
quotes: We evaluate the suitability of different quantum image representations using a toy quantum computing image reconstruction pipeline
Of the different quantum image encodings, we find that the QPIE encoding offers excellent algorithmic speedup without sacrificing image fidelity.
If a highfidelity image needs to be extracted from the quantum computer, then Nshots becomes intractably large.
The QPIE encodings may not be suitable for high-fidelity image analysis demanded by extended source structure or cosmological studies
we have demonstrated that in cases where lower image accuracy is tolerable quantum computing can be a powerful tool for real-time imaging.
existing.reader_inference: Fig. 3 reports that both FRQI and QPIE need a very large number of shots for under 10 percent error on random images, which sits uneasily with the unqualified Conclusion sentence.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum computing for radio interferometry remains completely unexplored.
quotes: QC for radio interferometry remains completely unexplored.
assertions.reader_inference: A novelty claim as of the paper's date; not checked here against the literature.

assertions.value: The authors state that their goal is to evaluate the quantum advantage for radio astronomy, and that they also consider quantum utility, the effectiveness and practicality of QC algorithms on current or near-term hardware.
quotes: Our goal is to evaluate the quantum advantage for radio astronomy, determining if QC algorithms and data encodings can ever achieve better performance than their classical counterparts.
We also consider quantum utility, the effectiveness and practicality of QC algorithms on current or near-term hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own goal and scope in Section 1.

assertions.value: The authors define quantum advantage as the case where algorithms designed to take advantage of QC offer exponential speedup compared to their classical counterparts.
quotes: In certain cases, algorithms designed to take advantage of QC can offer exponential speedup compared to their classical counterparts, known as quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the term in Section 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that classically, reconstructing the dirty image needs order N to the fourth power operations with the DFT, or order N squared times the base-2 logarithm of N operations with the FFT.
quotes: In the classical domain, this operation requires O(N4) operations using the DFT, or O(N2log2N) operations using the FFT.
assertions.reader_inference: Standard costs; the paper cites Brigham and Morrow (1967) for the FFT in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that a QPIE encoding of an image with N squared pixels needs only log base 2 of N squared qubits, so the QFT can be evaluated on this encoding with O(log2 N × log2 N) operations.
quotes: As a QPIE encoding of an image with N2 pixels only needs log2 N2 qubits, the QFT can be evaluated on this encoding with only O(log2 N × log2 N) operations.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QFT offers impressive speedup on the QPIE encoding, needing only O(g(N2)) = O(log2N × log2N) operations, outperforming both the DFT and the FFT, before the cost of state preparation and shots is counted.
quotes: The QFT offers impressive speedup, only needing O(g(N2)) = O(log2N × log2N) operations on the QPIE encoding, outperforming both the DFT and the FFT.
However, the cost of the state preparation and the number of shots needed to reconstruct the image must be taken account into the algorithmic complexity

assertions.value: The authors give the true complexity of the QFT, with the optimal QPIE circuit depth and the optimal number of shots, as O(M × ( f (N2) + g(N2))) = O(Nshots × log2N × log2N), and state that depending on the number of shots the QFT may not offer quantum advantage.
quotes: O(M × ( f (N2) + g(N2))) = O(Nshots × log2N × log2N) (8)
Depending on the number of shots needed to perform the measurement, the QFT may not offer quantum advantage.
If a highfidelity image needs to be extracted from the quantum computer, then Nshots becomes intractably large.
assertions.reader_inference: A derivation by the authors of an asymptotic bound, not a numbered theorem with stated assumptions.

assertions.value: The authors state that identifying a number of sources proportional to N squared needs Nshots = O(N2) shots, which has quantum advantage over the DFT but not the FFT.
quotes: In the case of identifying ∝ N2 sources in an image, Nshots = O(N2) shots are needed, which has quantum advantage over the DFT but not the FFT.

assertions.value: The authors state that evaluating quantum advantage is not as simple as comparing the algorithmic complexity of a classical and a quantum algorithm, because information must be extracted from the quantum state and measurement destroys the superposition.
quotes: Evaluating quantum advantage is not as simple as comparing the algorithmic complexity between a classical and quantum algorithm.
Information must also be extracted from the quantum state, and measurement destroys the superposition.

assertions.value: The authors state that the encoding cost may be bypassed with quantum random access memory, which would store input data in ancillary qubits and copy it instead of re-encoding, but that they consider their model realistic for near-term quantum computers.
quotes: We note that it is possible that this encoding cost may be bypassed with quantum random access memory
However, we consider our model in Fig. 6 realistic for near-term quantum computers.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no construction for the copy step and does not discuss the no-cloning theorem; the QRAM remark is speculative.

assertions.value: The authors state that the number of shots required will not change as quantum hardware improves, but can be improved with algorithmic development, and that it is advantageous to stay in the quantum domain as long as possible before measuring.
quotes: The number of shots required will not change as quantum hardware improves, but can be improved with algorithmic development.
for as long as possible before measuring the state, ideally performing additional data reduction so that fewer shots are required for analysis.

assertions.value: The authors state that for an interferometer with M antennas producing B = M(M − 1)/2 correlated visibilities, the QPIE encoding leverages superposition to achieve logarithmic compression, needing only log2(B) qubits.
quotes: an interferometer with M antennas will produce B = M(M − 1)/2 correlated visibilities
the QPIE encoding leverages superposition to achieve logarithmic compression, only needing log2(B) qubits

assertions.value: The authors state that classical data can be directly represented with binary encoding, so that for 64-bit floats representing complex-valued visibility data the entire image matrix can be encoded with 64 times N squared single-state qubits.
quotes: In the case where Vk are 64-bit floats representing complex-valued visibility data, the entire image matrix can be encoded with 64N2 single-state qubits.
assertions.reader_inference: Cites Cortese and Braje (2018) for binary encoding.

assertions.value: The authors state that preparing the FRQI state can be expensive, with a proposed circuit depth of O(N4) operations, which can be reduced to O(N2log2N) operations by introducing additional ancillary qubits.
quotes: Preparation of this state can be expensive, with a proposed circuit depth of O(N4) operations in Le et al. (2011), but can be reduced to O(N2log2N) operations by introducing additional ancillary qubits (Khan, 2019).

assertions.value: The authors state that several QPIE state preparation algorithms exist with circuit depths varying from O(log2 N × log2 N) to O(N4), as proposed by Zhang et al. (2021).
quotes: Several state preparation algorithms with circuit depths varying from O(log2 N × log2 N) to O(N4) are proposed in Zhang et al. (2021).

assertions.value: The authors state that the QFT circuit requires O(n2) gates, where n is the number of qubits in the input and output states.
quotes: The QFT circuit requires O(n2) gates, where n is the number of qubits in the input and output states.
assertions.reader_inference: Cites Nielsen and Chuang (2010) for the QFT.

assertions.value: The authors state that an implementation of the quantum FFT exists with lower computational complexity than the QFT, but it relies on the image being embedded in a basis encoding rather than the amplitude encoding used by QPIE.
quotes: An implementation of the quantum FFT algorithm exists which has lower computational complexity with respect to the QFT (Asaka et al., 2020), but it relies on the image being embedded in a basis encoding rather than the amplitude encoding used by QPIE.

assertions.value: The authors state that entanglement between states is necessary to achieve any significant computational speedup of QC over classical computing.
quotes: Entanglement between states is necessary to achieve any significant computational speedup of QC over classical computing
assertions.reader_inference: Cites Cortese and Braje (2018) and Jozsa and Linden (2003); the QPIE encoding is entangled across its row and column qubits only in general, which the paper does not discuss.

assertions.value: The authors state that the public can access only seven qubits on the IBM platform, limiting them to 4 × 4 pixels for the QPIE encoding, so they ran experiments on the QASM simulator, with no modeling of gate or measurement errors.
quotes: On the IBM platform, the public can only access up to seven qubits, limiting us to representations with only 4 × 4 pixels for the QPIE encoding.
We do not include any modeling of gate or measurement errors.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 states the paper's own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that complex phases cannot be directly measured from an encoded quantum state, so QC can reconstruct real-valued images from complex visibilities (the invert step), but predicting complex visibilities from images (the predict step) is not straightforward.
quotes: the measurement of a quantum state can only return the real magnitude of the phases
For radio interferometry, while we can use QC to reconstruct real-valued images from complex visibilities
The phases of complex probability amplitudes can not be easily read from a quantum state, limiting the applications of the inverse QFT for predicting visibilities from images.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.1 and the Conclusion state this limit of the approach.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum image representations must be re-encoded and remeasured multiple times to measure the state with high accuracy, and that this additional measurement error is a fundamental consequence of using QC compared to classical computing.
quotes: Quantum image representations must be re-encoded and remeasured multiple times to measure the state with high accuracy.
This additional measurement error is a fundamental consequence of using QC compared to classical computing.

assertions.value: The authors report, for images of different sizes with pixel values drawn from the uniform distribution U(0, 1), that both the FRQI and QPIE encodings offer comparable accuracy and require large numbers of shots, Nshots = Np2ix = N4 as printed, to reconstruct a random input image with < 10% error.
quotes: We generate images of different sizes, with pixel values drawn from the uniform distribution U(0, 1)
Both encodings offer comparable accuracy, and require large numbers of shots Nshots = Np2ix = N4 to reconstruct a random
input image with < 10% error.

assertions.value: The authors state that their mock source-finding test places random point sources convolved with a Gaussian kernel with σ = 1.5 pixels, adds random Gaussian noise, embeds the image in a QPIE, FRQI or Quantum Lattice representation, reconstructs it with varying numbers of shots, and fits 2D Gaussians to identify sources; a source counts as correctly identified within a 1.5 pixel distance of the true source.

We recursively fit 2D Gaussians to the reconstructed images to identify all of the sources.
We consider that a source is correctly identified if it is reconstructed with a 1.5 pixel distance from the true source.

In the second scenario, we have a single source with a high SNR=100

This model approximates searches for bright transient phenomena in the image domain.

els associated with low flux values, and therefore many shots
