The QPIE encodings may not be suitable for high-fidelity image analysis demanded by extended source structure or cosmological studies
assertions.certainty_reason: Sections 4.2 and 8 state what the paper does not cover.

assertions.value: The authors propose a novel variational quantum computing algorithm for self-calibration of interferometer visibilities, defined and implemented as a proof-of-concept using quantum variational circuits with QPIE encodings of the observed and model visibilities and a SWAP test, minimized by quantum gradient descent.
quotes: We also propose a novel variational quantum computing algorithm for self-calibration of interferometer visibilities
As a proof-of-concept, we define and implement a quantum algorithm for calibration using quantum variational circuits
We minimize this cost function with quantum gradient descent

assertions.value: The authors state that in the toy model they assume the interferometer geometry samples every point in Fourier space, allowing the visibilities to be represented with the 2D image QPIE encoding, and that for simplicity the gain terms are assumed to be real numbers.
quotes: In this toy model, we will assume that the interferometer geometry samples every point in Fourier space, allowing us to represent V using the 2D image QPIE encoding.
To simplify the analysis we assume that the gain terms gi are real numbers
assertions.certainty_reason: Sections 6.1 and 6.4 state the toy model's assumptions.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the quantum implementation the gradients are computed with the parameter shift rule, where the multiplier and shift are typically chosen to be m = 1/2 and s = π/2, and that the shifts are not infinitesimal as in finite differences.
quotes: where the multiplier m and the shift s are typically chosen to be m = 1/2 and s = π/2.
It is important to emphasize that in this approach, the shifts employed are not infinitesimal as typically used in finite differences.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QGD algorithm has a theoretical computational complexity of O(1) for evaluating the gradient, which provides significant advantages over a classical algorithm with a computational complexity of O(d), where d is the number of input parameters.
quotes: The QGD algorithm has a theoretical computational complexity of O(1) (Jordan, 2005) for evaluating the gradient, which provides significant advantages over classical algorithm with a computational complexity of O(d)
assertions.reader_inference: The cost function itself must be measured through repeated shots, as the paper notes next, so the O(1) gradient count does not remove the shot cost.

assertions.value: The authors define a hybrid quantum-classical calibration that evaluates the same SWAP-test cost function but, instead of QGD, uses the COBYLA minimizer on Scipy.
quotes: However, unlike the pure quantum algorithm, instead of using QGD to find the {gi} which minimize C({gi}), we use the COBYLA minimizer on Scipy.

assertions.value: The authors state that, due to the quantum uncertainty inherent in the state measurements, neither calibration method is expected to offer quantum advantage over a classical minimization algorithm, and that for this toy example a purely classical approach is more efficient and accurate.
quotes: Due to the quantum uncertainty inherent in the state measurements, neither calibration method is expected to offer quantum advantage over a classical minimization algorithm.
We note, however, that for this toy example using a purely classical approach is more efficient and accurate.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sections 6.3 and 6.4 state this limit of their own method.

assertions.value: The authors report, on randomly generated 2 × 2 radio sky images with QGD run for 1000 steps with η = 0.01, that the algorithm can successfully recover the gain factors with high accuracy, that 1000 steps take approximately two minutes on the quantum simulator, and that the hybrid approach converges in approximately five seconds and shows more stability.
quotes: We evaluate the performance using randomly generated 2 × 2 radio sky images.
QGD is run for 1000 steps and with η = 0.01.
The algorithm performs well and can successfully recover the gain factors with high accuracy.
Evaluating 1000 steps takes approximately two minutes on the quantum simulator. In comparison, the hybrid approach converges in approximately five seconds.
approach shows more stability.
assertions.reader_inference: The test uses a 2 × 2 image on a noiseless simulator; no error statistics are given in the text, only a histogram in the figure.

assertions.value: The authors give an approximate global error rate for a circuit with per-gate failure probability ϵ and circuit depth Dcirc as P(at least 1 gate fails) = 1 − P(all gates succeed) = 1 − (1 − ϵ)Dcirc, with the last term raised to the power Dcirc, and state that it ignores measurement and decoherence errors and should only be considered an approximate model.
quotes: P(at least 1 gate fails) = 1 − P(all gates succeed) = 1 − (1 − ϵ)Dcirc
The above approach also ignores the effect of measurement and decoherence errors, and thus should only be considered an approximate model of the true expected error rate.

assertions.value: The authors calculate that encoding a 4 × 4 image with the recursive initialization algorithm requires 30 Rz(θ), 30 S X and 14 CNOT gates, and that with the published error rates of the 5 qubit IBM Falcon r4T system the probability that the circuit fails is ≈ 15%.
quotes: We calculate that encoding a 4 × 4 image with the recursive initialization algorithm requires 30 Rz(θ), 30 S X and 14 CNOT gates.
Using the error rates above, the probability that the circuit fails is ≈ 15%.
The gate errors of the 5 qubit IBM Falcon r4T system have been measured through randomized benchmarking
assertions.reader_inference: A calculation from published gate error rates, not a run on hardware.

assertions.value: The authors calculate that encoding a QPIE image of 256×256 pixels requires a circuit with 131070 Rz(θ), 131070 S X and 65534 CNOT gates, that the probability this circuit fails is ≈ 100%, and state that the large circuit depth and high gate error rate make it impossible to encode the larger QPIE image.
quotes: We calculate that encoding a QPIE image 256×256 requires a circuit with 131070 Rz(θ), 131070 S X, and 65534 CNOT gates.
With such a deep circuit, the probability that this circuit fails is ≈ 100%.
The large circuit depth and high gate error rate make it impossible to encode the larger QPIE image.
assertions.reader_inference: This holds for the recursive initialization algorithm and the stated error rates.

assertions.value: The authors state that with the shorter circuits they describe, a 1024×1024 image can be encoded with a circuit depth of ∼ 100 gates, and with a gate error of ϵ = 10−4 the global failure rate will be ∼ 1%, but the large number of ancillary qubits required makes it impractical to run on current hardware.
quotes: a 1024×1024 image can be encoded with a circuit depth of ∼ 100 gates, and thus even with a gate error of ϵ = 10−4 the global failure rate will be ∼ 1%.
However, the large number of ancillary qubits required by this algorithm make it impractical to run on current hardware, and may be subject to additional decoherence errors.
assertions.reader_inference: The figure of about 100 gates is an estimate and is given without a derivation in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum utility of quantum image processing is limited to smaller image sizes by the noise and size of available hardware, and that QC hardware will still need to encode and process large input images to beat classical solutions.
quotes: Thus the quantum utility of quantum image processing is limited to smaller image sizes by the noise and size of available hardware.
However, QC hardware will still need to be able to encode and process large input images in order to offer better performance compared to classical computing solutions.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 7 states this limit.

assertions.value: The authors state that because the Fourier transform is a linear operation, a single Fourier transform on a large image can be split into multiple operations on smaller image sizes, and that it may be possible to perform equivalent input splitting with the QC.
quotes: a single Fourier transform on a large image can be split into multiple operations on smaller image sizes
It may be possible to perform equivalent input splitting with the QC, allowing hybrid QC algorithms to accommodate larger images.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that quantum computing has promising applications for image processing in radio astronomy, but is limited by the error rates and small qubit sizes of contemporary noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers.
quotes: Quantum Computing has promising applications for image processing in radio astronomy, but is limited by the error rates and small qubit sizes of contemporary noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers

assertions.value: The authors list as developments of particular interest for radio astronomy imaging: a quantum algorithm for gridding and/or degridding of input visibilities, an implementation of the QFFT for amplitude-based encodings such as QPIE, a quantum non-uniform discrete Fourier transform, an efficient algorithm for QPIE encoding of sparse images, and a quantum algorithm for deconvolution of the dirty image with the dirty beam.
quotes: A quantum algorithm for gridding and/or degridding of the input visibilities
An implementation of the QFFT that can be applied to amplitude-based image encodings such as the QPIE.
A quantum implementation of the non-uniform discrete Fourier transform
An efficient algorithm for QPIE encoding of sparse images
A quantum algorithm for deconvolution of S D with the dirty beam
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 8 states these as open problems.

papers.title_in_file: Towards Robust Benchmarking of Quantum Optimization Algorithms
papers.what_it_is: A guideline paper for fair benchmarks of quantum against classical optimization algorithms, tested on two Max-Cut scenarios and a Travelling Salesperson scenario.

existing.note: The stored value is right for scenario 1 (small random instances, 10 to 20 nodes, TTS metric) but the second half is too broad: in scenario 2 the branch-and-cut solvers did not win on the densest group, where simulated annealing, tabu search and D-Wave did better, and the result holds for the 351 instances embeddable on D-Wave under a 10 second limit. The conclusion's own wording is a summary.
existing.value: The authors report that simulated annealing had the lowest TTS on the small random Max-Cut instances of the first scenario, and that in the second scenario, under a time limit on the instances embeddable on D-Wave, the branch-and-cut solvers outperformed the others on larger and sparser graphs, but not on the most densely connected group, where simulated annealing, tabu search and D-Wave performed better.
existing.anchor: Section IV.A.1.f and IV.A.2.f, PDF p.8-9
quotes: As apparent from the results, SA performs best over all instances.
The heuristics SA, TS and DW perform significantly better on the highly dense graphs within the dataset.
However, for larger and sparser graphs outside this subset, the BNC solvers consistently outperform the others, exhibiting the lowest relative error and achieving the highest FOB.
An embedding on the DW hardware was found for 351 instances.

existing.note: The XY result is among the QUBO, HOBO and XY formulations only. The Grover permutation mixer is not in that TTS comparison: its TTS cannot be compared because of high-overhead circuits, and the paper says it is not clear how it compares.
existing.value: The authors report that among the QUBO, HOBO and XY-mixer QAOA implementations for the Travelling Salesperson Problem, the XY method performed best with regard to TTS, while the TTS of the Grover permutation mixer could not be compared with the others.
existing.anchor: Section IV.B.e-f and Section V, PDF p.10
quotes: The XY -Mixer method shows the best overall TTS performance.
Nevertheless, TTS comparison to the other approaches is infeasible due to the intricate (high overhead) circuits.
However, it is not clear how it compares in TTS with the other methods.

assertions.value: The authors state that the guidelines cover four points: application-specific algorithm choice with the most fitting formulation for every solver, the selection of benchmark data, a holistic figure of merit, and equitable hyperparameter training.
quotes: (1) application-specific algorithm choice, ensuring every solver is provided with the most fitting mathematical formulation of a problem
(4) equitable hyperparameter training to eliminate bias towards a particular method

assertions.value: The authors state that a key problem in existing benchmarking frameworks is the lack of equal effort in optimizing for the best quantum and, respectively, classical approaches.
quotes: A key problem in existing benchmarking frameworks is the lack of equal effort in optimizing for the best quantum and, respectively, classical approaches.

assertions.value: The authors state that prior comparisons predominantly rely on randomly generated problems or on instances crafted to suit the quantum hardware, and that some benchmarks lack a proper selection of use-case-optimized classical algorithms.
quotes: comparisons predominantly rely on randomly generated problems [3], [4] or even crafted instances suiting the quantum hardware [5]–[7]
sometimes lack the proper selection of usecase-optimized classical algorithms [5], [8]

assertions.value: The authors state that a classical branch-and-cut solver typically performs best when given a mixed-integer linear formulation of a constrained problem, rather than the penalty-term QUBO reformulation that quantum solvers require.
quotes: a classical BNC solver [13] typically shines in performance when posed with a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) [14] formulation of a constrained problem instead of the Quadratic Unconstrained Optimization Problem (QUBO) reformulation with penalty terms, required for quantum solvers

assertions.value: The authors state that the benchmark dataset should ideally be a diverse, real-world-inspired collection of instances, and that randomly generated instances may be needed when simulation or device limits cap the problem size.
quotes: The benchmarking dataset should ideally consist of a diverse and real-world-inspired collection of problem instances [15].
suitability considerations may require randomly generated instances, e.g., if the problem size is limited due to simulation or device restrictions [16].

assertions.value: The authors cite the no-free-lunch theorem as stating that no single algorithm can perform best on all possible problem instances, and give it as the reason many different heuristics exist.
quotes: As a consequence of the no-free-lunch theorem, which essentially states that no single algorithm can perform best on all possible problem instances, many different heuristics have been developed [20].

assertions.value: The authors describe simulated annealing as accepting a better neighbor always and a worse neighbor with a temperature-dependent probability, and name the geometric annealing schedule, which lowers the temperature exponentially each iteration with a decay hyperparameter between 0 and 1.
quotes: This candidate solution is always accepted (i.e., x ← x′) if it has a better objective value than the current solution

A popular choice is the geometric annealing schedule, which decreases the temperature Ti exponentially via Ti ← αTi−1, where T0 denotes the initial temperature and α ∈ (0, 1) the decay hyperparameter [27].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the simulated annealing method it benchmarks in Section II.

assertions.value: The authors describe the core of the commercial solvers CPLEX and Gurobi as the branch-and-cut algorithm: the cutting plane method first, then branch-and-bound if no integer solution is found.
quotes: Their core solvers are based on the branch-and-cut (BNC) algorithm [13], which starts by executing the cutting plane method [30], followed by the branch-and-bound algorithm [31].
If the cutting plane method is unable to find an integer solution, the branch-and-bound algorithm is started subsequently.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the solver family it benchmarks in Section II.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing two studies, that CPLEX and Gurobi have shown better results on average than open-source solvers, and they attribute this likely to optimized heuristics for cutting planes and branching.
quotes: CPLEX and Gurobi have shown to yield better results on average [38], [39], which can likely be attributed to their highly optimized (problem-aware) heuristics for selecting the cutting planes and the branching criteria.

assertions.value: The authors describe quantum annealing as built on the adiabatic theorem, and state that real hardware cannot run a truly adiabatic transition because of short-lived noisy qubits, so a faster-than-adiabatic transition is used and the process is repeated to sample from the output distribution.
quotes: the adiabatic theorem states that a quantum mechanical system remains in its lowest energy state when the changes applied to it are carried out adiabatically, i.e., slowly enough [41].
In reality, the adiabatic transition is generally disallowed because of short-lived noisy qubits.
Therefore, similar to TS and SA, one needs to repeat the process and sample from the output distribution.

assertions.value: The authors state that the cost landscape of any QUBO problem can be straightforwardly mapped onto the energy landscape of an Ising model.
quotes: the cost landscape of any Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem
can be straightforwardly mapped onto the energy landscape of an Ising model

assertions.value: The authors present the QAOA as a discretization of the annealing time evolution into p rounds, which approaches adiabatic evolution as p grows without bound, and state that low-p QAOA circuits are relatively short, which makes them of interest for NISQ-era devices.
quotes: By discretizing this continuous time evolution in p ∈ N rounds, one can derive the following quantum operation, i.e., the QAOA
U (β, γ) approaches adiabatic evolution for p → ∞
Low-p QAOA circuits are relatively short

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum annealers can currently tackle the largest problem instances because they offer the highest number of practically usable physical qubits, but that their analog form of computation makes them heavily susceptible to hardware noise.
quotes: While Quantum Annealers can currently tackle the largest problem instances as they offer the highest number of (practically usable) physical qubits, their analog form of computation makes them heavily susceptible to hardware noise.

assertions.value: The authors state that QUBOs cannot handle constraints, so constraints must be written as penalty terms that raise the energy of violating states, and that the QAOA, unlike quantum annealing, can encode constraint-satisfying properties directly.
quotes: QUBOs cannot handle constraints. Instead, constraints have to be formulated as penalty terms that disallow any constraint-violating states through higher energy contribution.
Nevertheless, it is possible to encode constraint-satisfying properties into the QAOA directly in contrast to QA [45].

assertions.value: The authors cite a QAOA mixer, the single-parity qudit XY-mixer, that allows only transitions between valid one-hot states instead of enforcing the one-hot constraint through penalty terms.
quotes: Instead of enforcing this constraint through penalty terms, Ref. [45] develop so-called single-parity qudit XY -mixers for QAOA, allowing only transitions between valid states.

assertions.value: The authors state that integer encoding of categories needs only a logarithmically growing number of qubits and is space-efficient, but that its cost functions are generally more difficult to implement and require higher-order qubit interactions (HOBO).
quotes: which requires only a logarithmically growing number of qubits ⌈log2 k⌉.
Therefore, it is space-efficient, but cost functions are generally more difficult to implement

assertions.value: The authors cite a permutation mixer by Bärtschi and Eidenbenz, built from a Grover-type diffusion operation, and state that its state-preparation circuit uses at most a number of gates of order k cubed and a number of layers of order k squared (exponents printed flat in the text layer: k3 and k2).
quotes: using at most O(k3) gates and O(k2) layers.

assertions.value: The authors state that the best mathematical formulation may differ between classical and quantum methods, that a benchmark should identify the best formulation for both, and that classical heuristics should always be considered because they may even beat branch-and-cut methods.
quotes: Thus, the best possible mathematical formulation may differ between classical and quantum methods [52]. The investigation should always focus on identifying the best formulation for both cases.
classical heuristics should always be considered, as they commonly have a fast runtime to obtain a single sample and may even beat BNC methods [53], [54].

assertions.value: The authors state that classical algorithms are not necessarily required when the goal is only to compare quantum algorithms against each other, but that reporting classical performance and including a naive baseline such as random sampling helps classify results.
quotes: the selection of classical algorithms is not necessarily required
it is beneficial to include a naive baseline, such as random sampling [2], [7].

assertions.value: The authors state that when real-world data is inaccessible, one should examine phase transitions of the problem and sample from regions where instances can be practically hard, and that pre-selecting hard instances by classical solver performance bears the risk of bias.
quotes: one should examine phase transitions of the investigated problem beforehand and make sure to sample from the areas in the configuration space where problems can be practically be hard [57].
However, this bears the risk of introducing bias, since only instances that are easy for another solver can be sampled due to no free lunch.

assertions.value: The authors state that a randomly generated dataset must be generated reproducibly and be diverse, and that if these criteria cannot be met the research must address the shortcomings transparently.
quotes: the randomly generated dataset must be generated in a reproducible fashion and should be diverse to prevent results from being non-generalizable across different problem instances.
the research must address these shortcomings transparently.

assertions.value: The authors state that which solver is considered best depends heavily on the choice of metric, which in turn depends on the intended purpose of the application.
quotes: Which solver is considered best heavily depends on the choice of metric, which, in turn, depends on the application's intended purpose.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the optimal solution is infeasible to obtain, relative performance against the overall best-found bit string is used and the metric is relabeled, and that a branch-and-cut solution has higher intrinsic value than a heuristic one because it can prove optimality.
quotes: Should the time to find the optimal solution be infeasible, we need to rely on relative performance.
the intrinsic value of a BNC solution is higher than the value of a heuristic solution because a BNC solver can prove optimality.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines how its metrics fall back to relative performance in Section III.C.

assertions.value: The authors define time-to-solution for a sampling solver as the time per sample multiplied by the number of repetitions needed to sample the optimal solution once with a probability of 99%, and state that runtime without finding the optimal solution cannot be considered TTS.
quotes: The remaining term is the number of repetitions required to sample the optimal solution once with a probability of 99%.
Algorithm runtime without finding the optimal solution cannot be considered Time-To-Solution (TTS).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines TTS in Section III.C.1 (Eq. 8).

assertions.value: The authors state that TTS is defined as the time for a single sample when the probability of measuring the optimal solution is 1 and as infinity when it is 0, and that to apply the metric the solver must sample at least a few optimal samples, otherwise TTS cannot be computed or is highly inaccurate.
quotes: In the edge cases p∗ = 1 and p∗ = 0, TTS is defined as tsolve/M and ∞, respectively.
To apply this metric, the solver needs to sample at least a few optimal samples.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this caveat of its own metric in Section III.C.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that when simulating quantum optimization circuits, the optimal-solution probability is exactly determinable from the statevector entries, which makes TTS useful, and that wall-clock time of a classical simulation is not meaningful because simulation overhead scales exponentially with the number of qubits.
quotes: p∗ is exactly determinable through the statevector entries, rendering TTS particularly useful [59].
for classical simulation of quantum circuits, measuring the wall-clock time is not meaningful since simulation overhead scales exponentially with the number of qubits.

assertions.value: The authors state that TTS requires the optimal solution to be known beforehand, which limits its applicability to classically challenging problems, and name Time-To-Target, with a threshold cost, as an alternative.
quotes: Another challenge for TTS is that the optimal solution has to be accessible prior to computing the metric. Because of this, the applicability to classically challenging problems is limited.
As an alternative, Time-To-Target (TTT) may be considered
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its own metric in Section III.C.1.

assertions.value: The authors motivate Best Solution Found within a given time frame for use cases where the optimal solution is not the aim, and state that heuristic and quantum solvers must be repeated until the time limit while branch-and-cut solvers can prove optimality and stop early.
quotes: we are not interested in which solver can find the optimal solution fastest but in which solver produces the Best Solution Found (BSF) within a given time frame.
However, BNC algorithms can already prove the optimality of a solution and terminate before all planned resources are used
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines BSF in Section III.C.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the BSF metric is simple and universal but prone to statistical fluctuations when the sample size is small, because the best sample sits at the edge of the distribution, so large sample sizes are required.
quotes: The advantage of this metric lies in its simplicity and universality.
This metric can be prone to statistical fluctuations, especially if the sample size is small.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this caveat of its own metric in Section III.C.2.

assertions.value: The authors define the Fraction of Overall Best solution found as how often a solver finds the overall best solution across instances, name the Pareto front of runtime and solution quality as a comparison tool, and define the approximation ratio as the normalized expectation value.
quotes: it can be beneficial to count how often a solver finds the overall best solution.
comparability can still be achieved by analyzing the Pareto front of runtime, solution quality, and optionally more metrics [60].
AR is defined as the normalized expectation value
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines these metrics in Section III.C.3 to III.C.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that a drawback of the approximation ratio is that algorithms need different time to create one sample, so it is not holistic, and that it is especially useful for comparing settings of the same heuristic or quantum solver.
quotes: A drawback of AR is that different algorithms need different time intervals to create one sample, therefore it is not holistic.
AR is especially useful for comparing different settings of the same heuristic or quantum solver
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this drawback of its own metric in Section III.C.5.

assertions.value: The authors define the feasibility ratio as the share of samples that do not violate the constraints, state that branch-and-cut solvers and feasible-space heuristics have a default ratio of 1, and state that it is vital when comparing formulations or mappings onto quantum hardware.
quotes: measures how many samples do not violate the constraints.
BNC solvers, as well as heuristics that only search the feasible space, will have a default feasibility ratio of 1.
The feasibility becomes vital when comparing different formulations or methods of mapping a problem onto quantum hardware [49].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the feasibility ratio in Section III.C.6.

assertions.value: The authors state that scaling analysis of a metric with problem size eases comparability when hardware is not directly comparable (QPU, CPU, GPU, cloud), and that scaling of quantum resources such as qubits and circuit depth matters because qubits are limited and error-prone.
quotes: The different analyses of the scaling behavior alleviate comparability issues when the hardware is not directly comparable, e.g., QPU, CPU, GPU, or cloud services.
it is vital to consider scaling quantum resources because the number of available qubits is vastly limited.

assertions.value: The authors state that hyperparameter optimization must be tailored to the metric and dataset, that consistent optimization effort across all algorithms is vital, and that unequal effort can markedly change comparative results.
quotes: It is essential to perform hyperparameter optimization tailored to a specific metric and dataset since outcomes can significantly vary with changes in problem size, type, or figure of merit.
Equally, ensuring consistent effort in optimizing hyperparameters across all algorithms is vital.
Differential levels of optimization effort can markedly affect the comparative results

assertions.value: The authors state that VQC parameter training should be attributed to the algorithm's runtime unless parameters are treated as a generalization task trained on an instance set separate from the benchmark set to minimize bias.
quotes: one has to attribute the full classical optimization process to the quantum optimization algorithm's runtime.
the instance set on which the parameters have been trained is not the same as the benchmark set to minimize bias.

assertions.value: The authors propose a lesser-parametrized generating function for the QAOA parameters, for example a low-degree polynomial, to regularize the expected pattern of decaying mixer angles and growing cost angles and avoid overfitting.
quotes: In the case of QAOA, decaying βis and growing γis are hinted by the connection to QA [43].
To regularize this pattern for the parameters and avoid overfitting, we propose the usage of a lesser parametrized generating function g for the QAOA parameters

assertions.value: The authors state that all numerical experiments ran single-core on an AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 5965WX, and that quantum annealing used D-Wave Advantage 5.4.
quotes: All numerical experiments are conducted on an AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 5965WX (single-core). For QA, we utilize D-Wave Advantage 5.4 (DW) [66].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Section IV, p.6.

assertions.value: The authors state that Max-Cut is NP-hard and that they formulate it as a QUBO in which an edge gives a negative contribution when its endpoints are assigned to different sets.
quotes: Max-Cut (MC) is an NP-hard optimization problem
giving a negative contribution if xi ̸= xj (assigned to different sets)

Real-world problem instances are not common at this size.

we can sample cuts that approximate the problem with AR r ≈ 0.878 [68].

we generate a second dataset solely used for hyperparameter optimization to avoid overfitting.
we use a degree-4 polynomial as a generator function and adjust the hyperparameters for each QAOAdepth p = 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 separately

TS did not significantly respond to changing tenure and restart parameters
To gather sufficient statistics for p∗, we perform 1000 runs for each heuristic.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the first scenario simulated annealing had the lowest TTS with and without overhead, that D-Wave and the Gurobi and CPLEX solvers had large overhead, that tabu search had almost constant TTS because almost every sample was optimal, and that local search showed the steepest runtime increase.

TS has almost constant TTS because almost every sample is optimal (see Fig. 3). LS shows the steepest runtime increase of all considered solvers.

assertions.value: The authors report that QAOA TTS measured in CNOT layers shows a U-shape for every problem size, indicating an optimal QAOA depth, that deeper circuits seemed always to deliver the optimal solution fastest on larger instances, and that the quantum solvers' scaling is shallower than that of simulated annealing and local search.
quotes: A U-shape is observable for every problem size, indicating an optimal QAOA depth.
For larger instances, deeper circuits always seemed to deliver the optimal solution fastest.
The examined scaling behavior of the quantum solvers (DW and QAOA) is shallower than both SA and LS.

assertions.value: The authors state that QAOA TTS in the first scenario is estimated by taking one CNOT layer as 1 microsecond because the circuit is simulated, and give a two-qubit gate time of 660 ns for current ibm_brisbane hardware.
quotes: a CNOT layer is estimated to take 1μs.
Current hardware (ibm_brisbane) has a two-qubit gate time of 660 ns.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this assumption of its own experiment in Section IV.A.1.e.

assertions.value: The authors state that the second scenario solves larger Max-Cut instances of 99 to 298 nodes and 110 to 2000 edges from MQLib, 371 instances in total, within a time limit of 10 seconds per instance, with BSF as the metric and the solvers of the first scenario except QAOA and Goemans-Williamson.
quotes: The second scenario assesses the effectiveness of solving larger-sized MC instances within a time limit of 10 seconds.
We examine MC problems consisting of 99– 298 nodes with 110–2000 edges from the MQLib [57].
In total, the dataset comprises 371 instances.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Section IV.A.2, p.7-8.

assertions.value: The authors state that the second scenario hyperparameters were tuned by grid search on a subset of 50 randomly selected instances, and that D-Wave's best configuration used the default annealing time of 20 microseconds with a chain strength factor of 0.2.
quotes: we optimize the hyperparameters on a subset of 50 randomly selected instances using grid search.
the most effective configuration involved utilizing the default annealing time of 20 μs in conjunction with a chain strength factor [74] of 0.2.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Section IV.A.2.d, p.7-8.

assertions.value: The authors state that an embedding on the D-Wave hardware was found for 351 of the instances and that the analysis concentrates on those instances.
quotes: An embedding on the DW hardware was found for 351 instances. Subsequent analyses will concentrate on these specific instances for comparative purposes.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison therefore covers only embeddable instances, which excludes the densest and largest graphs.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the second scenario Gurobi and CPLEX reached the lowest relative error in cut size, at most 10 to the power minus 4, across all groups except the first group of the most densely connected graphs, where they had significantly more outliers than simulated annealing, tabu search and D-Wave.
quotes: Gurobi and CPLEX achieve the lowest relative error in cut size (≤ 10−4) across all groups, except the first group
where Gurobi and CPLEX have significantly more outliers with a much higher relative error compared to SA, TS, and DW.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the first group of the densest graphs, simulated annealing reached a FOB of 1.0, tabu search about 0.99 and D-Wave about 0.95, while Gurobi and CPLEX reached about 0.82, and the authors read this as diminishing efficacy of the two commercial solvers on denser graphs.
quotes: While SA achieves a FOB of 1.0, closely followed by TS (≈ 0.99) and DW (≈ 0.95), Gurobi and CPLEX only achieve a FOB of ≈ 0.82.
signals a diminishing efficacy of both CPLEX and Gurobi in handling graphs of higher density.

assertions.value: The authors report that across all instances Gurobi slightly outperforms CPLEX, proving optimality for 2% more instances, and that local search had notably inferior performance, the highest relative error and the lowest FOB.
quotes: Across all instances, Gurobi slightly outperforms CPLEX, as it proves to find the optimal solution for 2% more instances.
The LS algorithm exhibits notably inferior performance compared to all other algorithms

assertions.value: The authors report that simulated annealing, tabu search and D-Wave perform significantly better on the highly dense graphs of the dataset, while on larger and sparser graphs outside that subset the branch-and-cut solvers consistently outperform the others with the lowest relative error and highest FOB.
quotes: The heuristics SA, TS and DW perform significantly better on the highly dense graphs within the dataset.
However, for larger and sparser graphs outside this subset, the BNC solvers consistently outperform the others, exhibiting the lowest relative error and achieving the highest FOB.

assertions.value: The authors state that an ILP formulation with lazy constraints solves a 100-node TSP in under a second on a laptop, which is out of reach for any current quantum solver since the QUBO formulation already needs 10 000 qubits, so the TSP benchmark compares only QAOA formulations.
quotes: solving a 100-node problem takes less than a second on a laptop, which is out of reach for any current quantum solver since the QUBO formulation already requires k2 = 10 000 qubits.
Therefore, we limit the TSP benchmark to only QAOA, comparing the performance of different formulations and implementations.

assertions.value: The authors state that the TSP benchmark compares QAOA with QUBO, HOBO, XY-mixer and Grover permutation mixer, simulated up to 6 locations (25 qubits in the QUBO and XY cases), on 150 circular instances plus 50 random instances per problem size, keeping only instances where a nearest-neighbor heuristic fails to find the optimum.
quotes: We simulate QAOA up to k+1 = 6, i.e., 25 qubits in the QUBO and XY case.
In total, our dataset consists of 150 circular instances from [77] with the parameter σ = 0.6, 1.0, 1.4 and 50 random instances per problem size.
We only consider problems in which the heuristic fails to find the optimal solution independent of the starting location.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Section IV.B.a-b, p.9-10.

assertions.value: The authors state that TTS for the TSP is counted in CNOT layers so that circuit complexity enters the comparison, but that precise CNOT counts for the permutation-based ansatz are inaccessible without a full circuit implementation and a large overhead is expected.
quotes: We chose TTS regarding CNOT layers since it also incorporates different circuit complexities into the comparison
the precise CNOT counts are inaccessible without full implementation of the circuit, but a large overhead is expected since USk is non-trivial [50].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its own measurement in Section IV.B.c.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the TSP benchmark the XY method performed best on TTS, especially at low QAOA depths p = 2 and 4, that at depth above 8 the plain QUBO and XY methods were comparable, and that low depths solved the problem faster on small instances for all methods, with this behavior inverting on larger ones.
quotes: reveals that the XY method performs best, especially considering low QAOA rounds p = 2, 4.
At p > 8, the plain QUBO and XY methods are comparable in performance.
low depths solve the problem faster throughout all methods. Nevertheless, this behavior inverts when more nodes are considered.

assertions.value: The authors report that the HOBO formulation is comparable in TTS until 5 locations, and that beyond that the larger number of terms increases the circuit depth per QAOA layer drastically.
quotes: The HOBO formulation is comparable up until k + 1 = 5; after that, ⌈log2 k⌉ = 3, and therefore, the number of terms increases the circuit depth per QAOA layer drastically.

assertions.value: The authors report that the permutation-based ansatz gave the best solution quality as expected because no infeasible solutions are possible, that its TTS cannot be compared with the others because of its high-overhead circuits, and that HOBO's near-equal solution quality is a pitfall since it ignores the circuit runtime, which supports using holistic metrics such as TTS.
quotes: we observe that the permutation-based ansatz returns the best results overall, as expected since no infeasible solutions are possible.
Nevertheless, TTS comparison to the other approaches is infeasible due to the intricate (high overhead) circuits.
This, again, proves why holistic metrics like TTS are useful and required for benchmarking.
assertions.reader_inference: The final sentence is the authors' reading of one benchmark, not a general result.

assertions.value: The authors state that the HOBO QAOA is only useful when the number of qubits is limited because TTS increases massively with the circuit depth of higher-order terms, that small-depth QUBO QAOA performs worst but improves considerably with depth, and that the XY-mixer shows the best overall TTS, while it is not clear how the Grover permutation mixer compares in TTS.
quotes: The HOBO QAOA is only useful when the number of qubits is limited since TTS increases massively due to the circuit depth of the higher-order terms.
Small-depth QUBO QAOA performs worst but increases considerably with depth p.
The XY -Mixer method shows the best overall TTS performance.
However, it is not clear how it compares in TTS with the other methods.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that a meaningful comparison must include state-of-the-art classical (branch-and-cut, heuristic) and quantum methods on real-world-derived or randomly generated instances, that the figure of merit must include the trade-off between runtime and solution quality, and that every algorithm's hyperparameters need equally careful tuning.
quotes: We highlight that a meaningful comparison must include state-of-the-art algorithms, both classical (BNC, heuristic) and quantum methods
a meaningful metric should include the trade-off between runtime and solution quality.
The hyperparameters of each solution algorithm need to be tuned with equal care to remove initial bias.

assertions.value: The authors state that every considered problem might add metrics or considerations that their general framework cannot encompass.
quotes: Every considered problem might add additional metrics or considerations that this general framework cannot encompass.
